title: Natural-born actor John Turturro: "I'm at a very fruitful time"
summary: He's gifted audiences with memorable appearances in more than 100 films and TV shows. Now, John Turturro, one of the great character actors, is playing a rare lead role in a charming and moving crime drama, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York."
story: Character actors like John Turturro never fail to leave their mark on screen. He's been commanding our attention in movies and on television for 46 years, always digging deep to deliver something memorable. Called one of the great character actors in the history of movies, Turturro responded with modesty: "Oh wow, I'll take that compliment. I'm not sure of it!"

Now 69, Turturro is doing some of his best work in Apple TV's "Severance," and on the big screen in a rare leading-man part, as a thief clinging to a world passing him by, in a charming and moving crime thriller, "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York."

"Within this tense sort of crime thriller, there's all this humanity and, like, tenderness," he said. "There's like this love story, and there's this guy who basically the world has changed around him. He's obsolete in some ways. So, how does someone like that survive in such a fast-changing world? I found it very evocative and moving."
To watch a trailer for "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York," click on the video player below.
We spoke to Turturro in his Brooklyn neighborhood. He's New York through and through – and is not a recluse. "I ride the train," he said.

Growing up in Hollis, Queens, his parents were a working-class couple with a penchant for drama. "They had kind of a very intimate relationship, and volatile at certain times," Turturro said. "When we used to watch 'The Honeymooners,' when I was really a little kid, my older brother, Ralph, used to call the show 'Mommy and Daddy.' It was, you know, an expressive, sometimes explosive household. So, you learn what size is, and what, also, quiet is within that."

They also loved movies, which made a lasting impression on their son. "I didn't go to the theater that much when I was young, but I watched the 'Million Dollar Movie,' and I watched all these great movies from the '30s, '40s, '50s. Those people opened up my brains, you know, whether it was Barbara Stanwyck, or Edward G., or Cagney, or Bette Davis, and they're, like, part of me."

The idea to become an actor formed watching Dustin Hoffman in "Midnight Cowboy": "I think it was the scene in the diner when he said, he was like, 'Oh, Joey, I only got 64 cents in my pocket.' And I was like, Who is this guy?"
And it was cemented with a Broadway musical: "Bob Fosse's 'Pippin,' I saw the commercial. I felt like someone was reaching their hand out to me, like to touch me. And I was like, Wow."

After college came a scholarship to get a master's at the Yale School of Drama, but not before getting cast in his first movie, "Raging Bull." It's described as a non-speaking part, but he got a little something in there – his first line, delivered to Robert de Niro.

During his career Turturro has worked opposite Paul Newman in "The Color of Money," and been directed by Robert Redford in "Quiz Show" – always searching for ways to unlock his character, like in "Miller's Crossing," the first of four films with the Coen Brothers.

The quirky voice of his character, Bernie Bernbaum, came from his accountant; the fear from a single day in his childhood. In a list of difficult scenes, Turturro's in "Miller's Crossing," where Bernbaum faces execution in the woods, is a difficult scene.

"I had one advantage," said Turturro. "When I was younger, I was a serious basketball player. My friends and I, we were coming home from a party and we had, like, a bike with a banana seat, you know, and the handle. We pulled into a schoolyard, and this guy was shooting baskets. There was three of us. So, he thought maybe we were going to try to steal something from him. It was late … he took out a gun. He put it right to my head, on my bike, and I was like, I was frozen. But I never forgot this feeling of having this gun pointed at my head."

He's collaborated nine times with Spike Lee, starting with "Do the Right Thing." Lee sent Turturro the script, then asked him which part he wanted to play. Turturro chose Pino, the racist son of the pizza shop owner.

Asked if he thought Lee wanted him to choose Pino, Turturro replied, "I think he was happy that I did. … One thing about me is like, I don't need to be liked if I'm doing a movie. What I need to do is to hold your attention, and I can, you know, surprise you. You know, I'm not looking to soften the edges with it, or even make it, you know, worse than it is. It is what it is."
He says he has seen that guy: "Yeah, and then you see it in all different forms. I think that's one of the unspoken things in our country, which has such diversity. It's something we grapple with."
When Turturro got the script for "The Big Lebowski," he noted to the Coen Brothers that the part was very small – to which they told him, You'll make something out of it. And he did.

"And I have to say, I was really embarrassed the first time I saw it," Turturro laughed. "I was laughing, but I was really embarrassed. I was like, I can't believe you put all this stuff in there! Because it's like we were friends and we were, like, seven years old and they said 'Come on over, let's do a show together.' You want to make your friend laugh!"

He also likes discussing the craft. "Let me tell you something, my man: I like being here and talking about acting and stuff," he said, "because for me, I'm a natural-born actor. That's just how it is and stuff."

Surprisingly, this natural-born actor doesn't have an Oscar nomination. There's some buzz that might change with "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York." And though awards would be nice, it's the work that matters to John Turturro.

Asked if he can measure success without awards, he replied, "Yes, I've been able to work and do interesting things and entertain people and maybe even make them think sometimes, or laugh or cry at different times, and take them away from their lives. So, I'm very, very appreciative of where I am. I want to keep that up, and I feel like I'm at a very fruitful time."

title: The inseparable legacies of Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner
summary: Lee Krasner has long been eclipsed by the shadow of her husband, Jackson Pollock. Now, a landmark show in New York City rewrites the story of the artists whose work and legacies were – aesthetically and personally – bound together.
story: The old farmhouse in the hamlet of Springs, N.Y., is easy to miss, if not for the sign for the Pollock-Krasner House and Study Center. Here, on the east end of Long Island, is where Jackson Pollock and Lee Krasner moved in the winter of 1945. And it was here where the Abstract Expressionists would send a seismic tremor through the art world.

It was their home and workplace. The married couple moved into a house with no plumbing or heating. "It was really a choice that they made to come out here, to go into isolation almost to really focus on the work," said the Center's director Matthew K. Ward.
Now an historical site run by Stony Brook University, the Pollock-Krasner House looks much as it did when Krasner died in 1984.
Ward showed us the custom-made speaker system that Pollack himself wired through a crawlspace. It has paint all over it. "Yeah, a lot of stuff here has paint all over it!" Ward laughed.
Krasner worked in an upstairs bedroom – small, but with a view of Accabonac   Creek. Pollock painted in the barn out back, but without an easel. "No – that's kind of Jackson's thing," Ward said.

Pollack stretched his canvases out on the floor, and would pour, drip, and splatter paint from above down onto the canvas. The floor is a work of art in itself. Ward said, "The way Pollock worked was so physical. I think we feel him through the floor."
The entire art world changed right here. In fact, Ward said, "The most modern work anybody had ever seen was made in this rustic space."
In 1949, Life magazine famously asked of Pollack, "Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?"
And yet, many people who might show up at the Pollack-Krasner House may ask, "Who's Lee Krasner?" After a new show at New York City's Metropolitan Museum of Art, no more.

In "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous," for the first time the two artists' careers are considered together. "We hopefully prime you for this idea of creative adjacency, two careers in parallel," said co-curator Brinda Kumar.

Early in the exhibition, you see Krasner's work on the left wall, and Pollock's through a portal. "You automatically understand, hopefully, how this dialogue is happening across the studio, across the lawn," Kumar said.
Pollock was born in Cody, Wyoming. Krasner was the child of Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn. So, why did they hit it off?
"A very good question!" said co-curator David Breslin. "I think for Pollock to meet someone who had that degree of sheer intelligence, bravado, I think her connections weren't a bad thing."

As to what attracted Krasner to Pollock, Breslin said, "I don't know if she needed him. She was drawn to his work. Who the man was who could have made that work almost became a riddle that she wanted to solve."

That riddle proved confounding. Pollock drank heavily, and had affairs. "She has this great line that says something along the lines of, 'Unfortunately, I have the fortune of being married to Jackson Pollock,'" said Breslin.
But in the mid-1950s, Krasner left for Paris. Jackson moved his girlfriend, Ruth Kligman, into the house and, said Breslin, "things kind of went to hell."
In 1956, Pollock died in a car crash. Kligman, also in the car, survived, but a friend did not.
Krasner went back to the house in Springs. She would aggressively promote Pollock's legacy as a painter, but she now took over his studio.
According to Breslin, "He dies; she's unleashed."
Kumar said, "Moving into the barn after Pollock's death allowed her to work on an unprecedented scale as well."
In the Sixties, she'd paint "Through Blue," "Right Bird Left," and "Combat."
"These are painted directly on the wall," Kumar said. "There's a kind of ferocity. And today if you go to Springs, you'll see the kind of ghostly outlines [from the canvases]."

Krasner lived and worked here for another 28 years after Pollock's death. Ward said, "This home is filled with ephemera that belonged to both of them. Lee wanted Jackson's legacy to live on just as her own, and she wanted them to live on together."

In effect, the exhibition "Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous" tries to rewrite history and change the mythology about these artists. Breslin said, "Our exhibition really has been an effort to say she's an equal."

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: How Gen X should practice "the art of aging"
summary: NPR health and science correspondent Allison Aubrey, author of the new book, "Your Turn: How to Create a Midlife You Love," talks about facing all the possibilities of life's third chapter.
story: NPR health and science correspondent and "Sunday Morning" contributor Allison Aubrey is out with a new book. "Your Turn" is what she calls it – and here she is to explain what she means...

If you're asking what's next in life, you're not alone. For the millions of Gen Xers like me, we've been in the trenches for decades with work and parenting. Now, everything's changing – our relationships, our responsibilities – as our kids begin to launch.

So, if life is lived in three chapters of learn, earn, retire, then it's time for us to start thinking about that third chapter. But I don't like the word retire, because it doesn't describe what this next stretch of life can be

When I was a teenager, I went to the Kentucky Derby. As I watched one horse that was stuck in the back of the pack suddenly make a bold move in the third turn and surge ahead to win the race, the fans loved it. My grandfather told me, "Allison, always watch the third turn. There's something exciting and unexpected that happens here."
"Why?" I asked.
"Well, because when you can see the home stretch," he told me, "a sense of urgency arises."
Ah-ha, there's a midlife metaphor! If not now, then when?

With that in mind, I took a sabbatical from my day job – I called it a "curiosity tour" – and I set out to find people who've made bold third-turn pivots: A nurse who sings lead vocals in a band; a lawyer who opened a bookstore; a shy editor who took up improv in her 60s; a counselor who teaches Shake Your Soul dance. Their stories reframe what's possible.

Research shows the best longevity hacks are not pills or products, but rather a sense of purpose, a sense of play. Creative pursuits, such as dancing, singing, painting, gardening, a love of literature or theatre, they don't just bring us joy; they appear to slow down aging.
A recent study finds engaging with the arts is as powerful as exercise to slow aging.
Of course, exercise and diet matter. But the art of aging invites us to imagine a blank canvas and create something new, like the people I met on my curiosity tour who are revving up, not retiring.

So, if you want to surge ahead in your third turn, rip up that old script of "learn, earn, retire." The new one is "learn, earn, return" – a return to the playful kid within. Listen to your intuition. This is how to find midlife momentum.
It's your turn.

title: AI agents detected inside customer bank accounts, report says
summary: Banks have detected personal AI agent activity inside customers' accounts as experts warn about the risks of oversharing with AI.
story: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized activity from third-party AI agents operating within their customers' online accounts, according to a new Axios report.
Some of the biggest financial institutions in the U.S. say customers have given their personal AI agents, which are unvetted by banks, access to their financial accounts.

"In a lot of cases, this is just going to be customers giving their username or password to an AI agent that the bank hasn't had a chance to vet yet, that goes against the bank's terms of service," Madison Mills, senior AI reporter for Axios, told CBS News. "In other cases, in our reporting, we did find evidence that appeared to look like agents taking actions in customer accounts that were not authorized."
Examples of agent behavior that a user never approved include the AI calling a bank with a complaint without first consulting the account holder.
"So, really a nightmare of AI agent activity for banks," Mills said.

To be sure, these agents weren't going rogue or hacking customer accounts and depleting their funds, Mills said. They were largely following user instructions without the bank's permission to transact on behalf of a human account holder.
"In no way cyberattacks"

White House AI czar David Sacks responded to the Axios report, saying in a post on X that there's a clear distinction between personal AI agents that help manage users' bank accounts and hackers deploying AI for nefarious purposes.

"There's a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks," he said. "Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf."
Sacks added, "This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks."

He believes banks should support the use of such user-authorized AI agents, but that if banks want to limit their access, they could grant AI agents "read-only" permission, meaning they could view a user's spending and other bank activity but couldn't take autonomous actions.

Under such circumstances, an agent could view your purchases and opine on whether you're spending too much money eating out, for example. But it couldn't make a purchase on your behalf or take any other action.
"Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully," he said.
Mills noted that it's an industrywide problem facing dozens of financial institutions as they race to curb AI agents' access to customer accounts.
Banks taking action
Some banks said they're taking action to make their customers aware of the risks of sharing their credentials with AI.

"Customers should not give their username and passwords to anyone. We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers to meet customers' needs while keeping their accounts safe," a Chase spokesperson told CBS News.
JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon expressed concern about AI agents taking actions in customers' accounts on the company's Oct. 13 earnings conference call.
"We're not going to allow just any outside agents to come in inside the company because it's just too risky for clients and for JPMorgan," he said.
Charles Schwab's CEO earlier this month said the company has been blocking unauthorized agents, according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Morgan Stanley said it had not observed any unauthorized AI agent activity across its platforms.
Bank of America and Wells Fargo did not immediately respond to CBS News' requests for comment on the matter.

title: Trump says new fuel supply push will lower prices. Will it work?
summary: The Trump administration said using the DPA funding will increase refining output and lower fuel prices for Americans. Experts are skeptical.
story: President Trump on Thursday said his administration will invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production in the U.S., the latest effort from the administration to lower fuel prices.

The Defense Production Act, or DPA, is a Korean War-era law that allows the president to use loans, purchase commitments and other mechanisms to incentivize the production of critical materials and goods.
The announcement follows a meeting President Trump had with refiners to discuss immediate steps to bring more capacity online, a White House official told CBS News.

In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Energy said the DPA funding will increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day and lower fuel prices for Americans, who have been paying more than $4 a gallon on average for gas over the last three months.

The new plan to increase fuel production comes as polling shows a majority of Americans are pessimistic about the U.S. economy amid a growing affordability crunch. Crude oil prices have continued to climb, hitting their highest level this week since May.
On Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was $116 a barrel, up 2.6%, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was around $103 a barrel, up 3%.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline stood at $4.29 on Friday and $6.32 for diesel, according to AAA. Those prices represent a 40% and 74% jump from a year earlier, respectively.

Passed in 1950, the DPA was originally aimed at boosting supplies for national defense purposes. However, Congress has broadened its application to address natural hazards, terrorist attacks and other national emergencies.
Will the measure be effective?
Experts told CBS News that invoking the DPA is unlikely to do much to lower fuel prices.
"I don't think that's really going to have any impact," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News in an email.

There are some potential upsides: DPA funds could speed up some refining expansions, Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News. However, he said any short-term benefits are unlikely.
"There is no slack in U.S. refining, so production can't be added regardless of political will," Kloza said. He said it typically takes months and calendar quarters to bring units back to service.
The White House official said the DFA funds will help expand capacity and modernize existing infrastructure, which is much faster than building a new refinery.
The U.S. produces more fuel than it consumes. Oil prices, however, are set on the global market, where the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted shipments, pushing prices higher.

The U.S. produces around 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel oil, a category that includes diesel, per day but consumes only about 3.6 million barrels per day, experts have noted. The U.S. also produces 9.5 million barrels of gasoline per day, more than the 8.9 million consumed domestically.
The U.S. exports about 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day, Kloza, told CBS News.
A spokesperson for the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, a trade association that represents refiners, said it appreciated the Trump administration's focus on the importance of refineries.

"Our country's 128 operating refineries produce more fuel in the United States than we consume," the spokesperson said in an email. "They are running all-out to keep Americans supplied and the global economy moving despite major disruptions and actual fuel shortages in other parts of the world."

title: Anthropic previews Claude Duet personal AI agent for subscribers
summary: Anthropic said Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for paying subscribers. Here's what it can do.
story: Anthropic has joined the race to develop AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of humans with Claude Duet, a new app it previewed this week.
The agent competes with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, rival developers' agents that are already popular with consumers.
Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for Claude U.S. Pro and Max subscribers, according to Anthropic.
What can Claude Duet do?
Claude Duet works as a "proactive agent" for human customers, taking autonomous actions to complete tasks assigned to it.

"It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said, noting that it was designed for professionals and small business owners "with more on their plates than they can track."
Anthropic said Claude Duet's utility lies in its superior judgment, describing it as smart enough to know what to prioritize and which tasks require a user's attention.

Each morning, Claude Duet sends its user a daily brief outlining the day's most important items. For the agent to have context, it must be connected to a person's apps, like their email accounts and calendars. Some security professionals have raised concerns about new AI agents' access to such information, warning users to limit how much they share.
"Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work," Anthropic said.
What about security issues?
Anthropic highlighted built-in security measures that it says make the app safe to use, noting that the agent never directly sees a person's passwords or sign-in tokens.

Claude Duet can also handle administrative tasks like scheduling meetings and creating financial or sales forecasts. It can build web apps, too, Anthropic said. It can draft job postings or make purchases on a business owner's behalf.
Anthropic researchers who have tested the app have used it to manage their to-do lists, build apps, schedule interviews and more.
How do you sign up?
Anthropic said people can sign up on the waitlist at its Claude Duet product page.
Invitations are issued in waves, and the product is only available in the U.S. during its research preview, the company said.
"We're adding people gradually, and you'll get an email when it's your turn," the company said.

title: What to know about ACA open enrollment this year
summary: As open enrollment for Affordable Care Act health insurance kicks off, consumers face rising premiums, additional identity checks, and fewer brokers.
story: Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.
Shoppers need to plan accordingly.
Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts start earlier, and some states are already allowing "window shopping" to check premium rates.

A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.

But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.
Have your ID ready

One of the biggest changes will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents via requirements aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.

The new rules, outlined in a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services FAQ, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.

For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.

Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed "high-risk" must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as "high-risk" first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.

Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because "someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer."

The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.
The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned "that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing" and may just give up and not get insured.

Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian's help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver's license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.

"Some people may have trouble not because they're not real, but because they don't have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names," said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.
She said the changes might "be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles."
There may be fewer brokers

CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.

CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of "significant compliance concerns" in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out "hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers" this year.

Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients' coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.
"Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense," he said. However, in the short term, "I don't know if they care about the chaos it will cause."

That's because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he's unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.

He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.
"They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long," Fine said.

Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.

"Just because you're a new agent doesn't mean you are fraudulent," said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. "All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won't be able to work."

It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown's Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. "If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early."
Costs will continue to be an issue

This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.
But most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will still receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.
The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.
This helps offset premium increases.

"For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same," said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst for HealthInsurance.org. "That's not to say it's great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that."
But there are other factors at work, too.

Last year's average premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers' fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs, inflation, and labor shortages.
For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.

Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.

"The biggest issue we will face is affordability," said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. "There definitely will come a breaking point for people."

Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.

"If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity," Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.

That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.

Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: Public Service Loan Forgiveness overhaul dropped, filing shows
summary: Advocates for student loan borrowers said the move will benefit workers who dedicate themselves to public service.
story: The Trump administration has halted its efforts to overhaul the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program, ending a plan that could have blocked some U.S. workers from tapping the popular lending program.

In a filing on Wednesday, the Trump administration said it was dropping its appeal of a June 30 federal court ruling that found the overhaul unlawful, without providing an explanation for its decision. Advocates for student borrowers hailed the step. Dan Zibel, chief counsel of the advocacy group Student Borrowers, called it a "significant victory for millions of Americans who have dedicated their careers to public service."

The proposed rule changes to the federal Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PLSF) program, originally proposed in August 2025, would have prohibited people from participating if their employer engaged in certain illegal activities. The proposed revamp said that employees who work for organizations that support terrorism, violate immigration laws or are involved in what the rule described as the "chemical and surgical castration or mutilation of children" would be barred.
The Department of Education didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Here's what to know about the change.
What is the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program?

The PLSF is aimed at people who work for government agencies, public schools, fire and police departments, public hospitals, and nonprofits. The idea is to provide a pathway to student loan forgiveness for people who work in public service. The program cancels outstanding debt for eligible borrowers who make 120 monthly payments, or 10 years of participation.
Almost 720,000 federal student loans were discharged through the program between 2018 and mid-2025, according to the Education Data Initiative, which collects data about the U.S. education system.
What did the Trump administration want to change?

At the time the Trump administration announced the new rule, Department of Education Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent said the rationale for revamping the PLSF was "supporting public servants who strengthen their communities and serve the public good, not benefiting businesses engaged in illegal activity that harms Americans."

The rule sought to disqualify applicants from the program if their employer engaged in "a substantial illegal purpose." It included a list of activities such as violating immigration laws, terrorism, trafficking, violating state laws or "violence for the purpose of obstructing or influencing federal government policy."
The rule was finalized in October 2025.
Who challenged the overhaul?

The rule was challenged in the courts by multiple nonprofits and municipalities, including Public Citizen Litigation Group and Student Defense on behalf of the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the American Immigration Council and cities including Albuquerque, New Mexico, Boston and Chicago.
The groups argued that the rule gave the Department of Education excessive latitude in deciding whether an organization was engaged in "a substantial illegal purpose."

Just before it was set to take effect in July, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun in Massachusetts vacated the rule, saying it overstepped the Education Department's authority and threatened to violate First Amendment protections for free speech. On the same day, District Judge Amir Ali in Washington issued a similar ruling in a case brought by nonprofit organizations.
Nonprofit leaders on Thursday said the administration's decision to drop the appeal will provide relief to many public servants.
"With the appeal dismissed, the court's order vacating the rule stands, and PLSF remains as Congress designed it," Diane Yentel, CEO of the National Council of Nonprofits, said in a statement.

She added, "This outcome gives nonprofit employees the certainty that the loan relief they've earned through years of public service will be there for them, so they can keep doing the work that strengthens the communities they serve."

title: Nasdaq dives 750 points as investors reassess AI spending
summary: Investors are fretting over the massive debt AI companies are relying on to finance data center and chip spending, Wall Street analysts say.
story: Stocks slid sharply on Thursday amid mounting concerns over whether massive investments in artificial intelligence will pay off and high oil prices.

Shortly before the close of trading, the Nasdaq Composite Index, where many technology companies exposed to AI are listed, tumbled 751 points, or 2.8%, before rebounding slightly to close 694 points lower at 26,009. The broader S&P 500 fell 1.2%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average eked out a small gain of less than 0.1%.

Investors are increasingly worried about the enormous debt AI companies are taking on to finance data center spending and whether the companies will generate the profits investors are banking on, according to Wall Street analysts.

"AI growth is dependent on capex (this is one of the most capital-intensive industries ever), and since capex is dramatically outpacing op. cash flow, companies are reliant on the largess of equity and debt investors to underwrite all the spending, but lately those markets are becoming increasingly less accommodating," Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note to investors on Thursday.
Slowing debt issuance as the credit environment tightens could hinder companies' ability to finance the AI infrastructure buildout, Crisafulli added.

The Brookings Institution, a nonpartisan think tank, estimates that it will cost more than $10 trillion to develop AI infrastructure between 2025 and 2032. That would amount to the largest tide of investment in U.S. history, dwarfing the construction of the railroads in the 19th century and, more recently, the dot-com boom, according to Carl Weinberg, chief economist for the financial market analysis firm High Frequency Economics.
Although many of the big players driving the AI boom remain highly profitable, investors are reassessing those massive costs as their stock prices soar.

The drop in markets on Thursday came amid a series of earnings reports that showed mixed performance results. Meta Platforms, which is pushing its Muse AI agent, lost 7% after revenue topped estimates while profit fell short. Tesla slipped 3.1%, with the electric vehicle company reporting stronger-than-expected summer profits but weaker revenue than analysts expected.

A rise in oil prices, driven by concerns about escalations in the war in Iran, was also weighing on stocks on Thursday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $99.21 a barrel, up 2.1%, while Brent crude, the international standard, was trading at around $113 a barrel, up 3.7%.

title: What to know about the PHP bug affecting 70% of world's websites
summary: AI was used to uncover a security weakness that affects most of the world's websites, researchers said. Here's what internet users should know.
story: Hackers could exploit weaknesses in a widely used programming language for websites, online platforms and other technology services to steal users' information and cause other problems, cybersecurity researchers warn.

The programming language PHP, short for "Personal Home Page," powers up to 70% of the world's websites and web applications, including those used by government agencies, social media platforms such as Facebook and sites including Wikipedia.

The bug, dubbed PHP2Shell, can target two security flaws in PHP,  according to Voldemaras Kadys, head of security at Mediatech. Those weaknesses could enable cybercriminals to seize control of unprotected website servers, install malware, pilfer customer data and even take sites down completely.
"The potential impact of these vulnerabilities may be huge, as most websites run on PHP," he said in an email.

The flaws in PHP were discovered when security researchers used an OpenAI artificial intelligence model to identify the problem, Wall Street Journal reporter Robert McMillan, who first reported on the PHP security issue, told CBS News.
"There are a lot of sites that I don't think even know that they have a problem, and they may find out the hard way."
What should consumers know?
Consumers' personal information could be vulnerable if they have an account with an online store or booking platform whose site uses PHP and is exposed to the bug.

"For regular internet users, simply visiting a PHP website doesn't necessarily mean their device will be compromised," Kadys explained. "The risk is that attackers may exploit a website that holds their personal information. For example, if a user has an account with an online shop, attackers may be able to hack that website through this PHP vulnerability and extract the information the user has stored there, such as their email address, physical address, name and date of birth."
But just because a site is vulnerable doesn't guarantee that a breach has occurred or will occur.

"There's no reason to stop browsing or shopping online, but users should still be extra cautious about suspicious messages because we don't know what kind of data hackers may have stolen through this vulnerability, and from which websites," he added.
Racing hackers

Andrés Guerrero-Saade, vice president of intelligence and security research at SentinelOne, told CBS News that the incident illustrates "how AI is accelerating the ability of vulnerability researchers" while also boosting bad actors' capacity to exploit security flaws.

The time between a vulnerability being detected and a fix being released is crucial for cybersecurity experts, he added. Yet that vital window of time has been shortened by AI, allowing cybercriminals to move much faster today than in the past.
"That whole gap between the patch being available and attackers getting to exploit that before anybody patches, that's the whole game essentially," Guerrero-Saade said.
In a post on X, the FBI's cyber threat division encouraged any organization that can't immediately patch its sites to temporarily take them offline.

The PHP Foundation, which includes tech developers who work on securing the programming language, said on Wednesday that it had released fixes for the vulnerabilities, along with instructions on how to update systems.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems," the group said.

The discovery of the flaws highlights the battle between security professionals and hackers in using AI to spot potential holes in organizations' technology systems. In this case, security researchers were the first to uncover the bug, which had existed for at least a decade, McMillan noted.

"People knew something weird was going on. But no one could really find a way to write an exploit — of turning a bug that might cause a computer to crash into something really bad that would allow somebody to run software that they weren't supposed to be able to run on a computer," he said.

title: Hegseth bans use of nonpublic info for bets on U.S. military ops
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the ban applies to classified and unclassified information and includes prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has banned Defense Department personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military operations, according to a memorandum obtained by CBS News.

In the Oct. 20 message to senior Pentagon leadership and combatant commanders, Hegseth said the prohibition would apply to classified and unclassified information and specifically includes prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi, which are named in the memo.
The defense secretary warned that financial transactions on prediction markets could expose sensitive military movements to foreign adversaries and endanger American troops.

"Make no mistake why this matters. Our enemies watch movements in these markets," Hegseth wrote. "When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal."

Hegseth warned that foreign intelligence services could analyze betting activity to anticipate American military movements, targets and timing of an operation. The memorandum said violations could result in administrative disciplinary or criminal action under federal law or the Uniform Code of Military Justice, the laws and regulations governing the U.S. military.

The directive follows growing scrutiny of service members participating in military-related prediction markets. In April, a U.S. Special Forces soldier involved in the military operation that captured Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro was arrested after allegedly betting on Maduro's removal from office before news of the raid was made public.

Federal investigators believe U.S. Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke made bets of more than $33,000 on the prediction market Polymarket within hours of President Trump's announcement in January that Maduro had been captured. The bets resulted in winnings of more than $409,000.
The soldier entered a not guilty plea in New York federal court.
This story published first on CBS News at 3:21 p.m. on Oct. 22, 2026.

title: Airbnb limits guest chores like laundry, drawing host backlash
summary: The new policy prevents hosts from asking guests to strip beds, start a load of laundry and other tasks that "require significant effort or time."
story: Airbnb is updating its rules to shield visitors from onerous cleaning tasks it says could negatively impact their stay.

The new policy, announced this week, prevents hosts from asking guests to strip beds, start a load of laundry and other household chores Airbnb says "require significant effort or time" and would typically be performed by a cleaner.
These tasks could lead guests to write negative reviews, Airbnb said, which ultimately hurt the property owner.

The new policy sparked backlash among some hosts, with more than 5,000 people signing a Change.org petition calling on Airbnb to reverse the rules. The signatories argued that the policy goes too far and is "unreasonable."
Requiring a cleaner to pick up the slack could hike expenses for hosts, which could ultimately be passed on to guests in the form of higher accommodation prices, the petition says.
"These are not professional cleaning duties," the petition says. "They are ordinary aspects of living responsibly in somebody else's property."
What are the new rules?

The online booking platform clarified which requests are "reasonable" as part of a new policy it unveiled on its website. The new rules apply to reservations booked on or after Nov. 20, according to Airbnb.

In some cases, it's a fine line: hosts can ask guests to put used dishes in the sink, but they can't ask them to wash or put away dishes. They can request that guests separate trash and recycling, but can't ask guests to deposit garbage at an off-site facility.
"When adding a request, remember that most guests want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said on its website.

Airbnb said that if hosts repeatedly violate the rules, the rental company could reduce the visibility of their listing page or issue a notice to guests on the listing page about the host's violation.

title: Childcare costs are growing faster than rent in the U.S.
summary: A growing share of American families are having to shell out more than $2,000 a month for childcare services, new data shows.
story: The rising cost of childcare in the U.S. is vying with food prices and healthcare expenses in straining household budgets.

Nearly 8% of families are spending more than $2,000 per month on childcare services, including daycare, nanny services and other programs. That's more than double the share of households that spent that much just three years ago, according to new research from the Bank of America Institute.

In September, the cost of daycare and school-related fees rose faster than other essential expenses, such as rent and medical care, compared to the same period a year ago, according to federal labor data.

Families nationwide spent an average of 8% of their monthly incomes on childcare services in September, BofA found. Under federal guidelines, childcare is considered affordable when it consumes no more than 7% of household income.

Assuming a family spends $24,000 annually on childcare, it would need to earn roughly $343,000 to remain below the 7% threshold. In 2025, median household income was $87,460, according to Census Bureau data.
Lower- and middle-income families spend nearly 9% of their annual incomes on childcare payments, while higher-income households spend 7.3%, according to BofA.

Along with facing rising childcare costs, workers have also seen slowing wage growth, heightening the financial pressure on many families, Economic Policy Institute economist Elise Gould told CBS News.
Separate research from AARP shows that families are turning to grandparents, who provide $172 billion per year in direct financial assistance.
Where are childcare costs growing fastest?

In some parts of the U.S., childcare fees are rising even faster, according to BofA. In September, median childcare costs rose fastest in Nashville, Tennessee, followed by Jacksonville, Florida, and Phoenix, Arizona, compared to the same period a year ago, according to BofA's analysis.

"There's been an increase in domestic migration to these areas," BofA Institute economist Taylor Bowley told CBS News, noting that an increase in demand for childcare services is putting pressure on prices.

A shortage of childcare workers also appears to be driving up childcare expenses. Employment in the sector fell 0.7% in September compared to one year earlier, making it harder for providers to deliver such services.
"You see job growth falling and price pressures creeping in, leading to a bit of an availability problem," BofA Institute senior economist David Tinsley told CBS News.

A lack of affordable childcare disproportionately affects women's employment opportunities, according to the researchers. Women are more likely than men to take on childcare responsibilities, according to data from the American Time Use Survey.
"Beyond childcare being a household expense, it's a form of economic enablement," Bowley said.

title: iPhone Duo already backordered until 2027 as pre-order sales soar
summary: Consumer demand for Apple's first foldable phone is strong despite the device's hefty $1,999 price tag.
story: Apple is seeing strong demand for its new foldable iPhone, with supplies quickly selling out after pre-order sales opened on Friday.

"Apple opened iPhone Duo pre-orders this morning, and the early read looks robust in our view, with demand for Cupertino's first foldable running well ahead of supply out of the gates," Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note.

The pre-order window for the Duo opened on Friday at 8 a.m. ET on apple.com and in the Apple Store app. Within minutes, the estimated delivery of the phone was pushed back past Oct. 23, the device's official launch date, and into next year. As of Friday afternoon, the Apple phone was backordered until late January.
"It's been 3 minutes, and it's sold out at every store around the NYC/CT area," Max Weinbach, an analyst for the market research firm Creativestrat, said on X.
Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how many pre-order requests it received.
When the Duo officially launches on Oct. 23, Apple said it will have some inventory at its stores, but noted that supply could sell out quickly.

"On Friday morning, our teams look forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores to experience iPhone Duo and the incredible iPhone line-up for themselves," an Apple spokesperson said in an email. "Apple Stores will have limited iPhone Duo available for walk-in customers, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible."

Apple's new CEO, John Ternus, announced the iPhone Duo last month. The Duo lets users split the screen to use two different apps on the device, or two windows of the same website for uses such as comparison shopping.

Prices start at $1,999 for a device with 256 GB of storage. When folded, it's about the size of a passport. The full display is the largest of any Apple phone, resembling more of an iPad than an iPhone.
Ternus also announced the iPhone 18 at Apple's annual fall showcase, which went on sale last month.

Ives thinks demand for the Duo will remain strong into 2027, with many iPhone users planning to upgrade. He projects Apple will sell around 10 million Duos in the next few quarters and up to 25 million in 2027.

title: Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California over wealth tax
summary: Zuckerberg has agreed to remain in California for eight years as part of a board-approved plan to create new shares he can sell to pay a proposed wealth tax.
story: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg threatened to move out of California if residents of the state approve a first-of-its-kind billionaire wealth tax when voters head to the polls on Nov. 3, the company said in a new regulatory filing.

Because of his concerns over the wealth tax, Zuckerberg told Meta that he was "evaluating relocating his primary residence outside California and that steps toward any such relocation, including any listing of his residential real estate in California on the market, would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees and, accordingly, raise questions for management of the company going forward," the filing states.

Meta said that because Zuckerberg's presence near the company's Menlo Park, California, headquarters is "critically important" to its success, the company took an unusual step: Its board approved a new class of nonvoting common stock that he can sell to raise cash to pay the wealth tax, if voters approve it.
Without that change, Zuckerberg faced the prospect of having to sell voting shares to raise funds to pay the tax, which would have reduced his control of Meta.

As a result of that decision to issue new stock, Zuckerberg has told Meta he will commit to remaining a California resident for eight years. If Meta moves its headquarters to another state, Zuckerberg will move to that jurisdiction, according to the regulatory filing.

The disclosure highlights the public debate over the proposed billionaire wealth tax, known as Proposition 40, which will be on the Nov. 3 ballot in California. Under the proposal, the tax would impose a one-time 5% state tax on billionaire wealth — about $12.4 billion of Zuckerberg's estimated $247 billion net worth, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

The company believes "it is critically important to keep Mr. Zuckerberg in a leadership position with our company and that he continue to reside in and manage the company from our headquarters in California to ensure his continued ability to effectively drive our performance during this era of unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry," Meta said in its filing.

The billionaire tax is aimed at raising $100 billion from the state's wealthiest residents, with the money earmarked for shoring up California's healthcare system. Stanford University economists have questioned whether the tax could backfire, given that several billionaires have already moved out of the state. The economists said that could result in lower projected wealth taxes and reduced overall income tax collections.
Nonvoting Class C shares
Creating a new stock class isn't only designed to keep Zuckerberg near Meta's headquarters, according to the filing.

The publicly listed, nonvoting Class C common stock, which will become effective in January, is also intended in part to boost the company's ability to raise capital for AI infrastructure investments. It will also use the new stock to raise capital, compensate employees, make acquisitions and for other general corporate purposes.
"Meta plans to issue nonvoting shares to fund AI investments without diluting CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control," said Andrew Rocco, stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research.

title: Warren warns of "food insecurity crisis" from SNAP cuts and prices
summary: Sen. Elizabeth Warren is urging the U.S. Department of Agriculture to reverse cuts to the food-stamp program as consumers shoulder $22 billion in additional food costs.
story: Americans are facing a "food insecurity crisis" after shouldering an additional $22 billion in food costs due to rising inflation and billions of dollars in food-stamp cuts, according to Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

In an Oct. 21 letter to U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, the Massachusetts Democrat said that the combination of rising food prices and cuts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program has created a "one-two punch" for millions of households.
Warren also asked the USDA to work with lawmakers to reverse food-stamp policies that have resulted in 5.2 million people losing SNAP benefits since July 2025.

SNAP enrollment, now at its lowest level since 2019, could shrink in the coming months as additional changes to the program take effect, according to anti-hunger experts. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), a tax and spending law signed into law by President Trump in 2025, expanded SNAP's work requirements and shifted more of the program's costs onto states. Those changes have created new hurdles for enrollment, according to experts.

The USDA halted its annual study on food insecurity in 2025, saying at the time that the report was "redundant, costly [and] politicized." But a May analysis from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found "a remarkable increase in food insecurity, particularly among lower-educated and lower-income households and households with young children."

The New York Fed found earlier this year that 10% of U.S. families reported they didn't have enough food and that their children sometimes missed meals, more than double the 4% share in 2020. Almost 20% of families with annual income of less than $50,000 reported not having enough food, up from about 7% six years ago.

"My office developed a 'food misery index' to measure how much the combination of rising food prices and declining SNAP participation is costing American households," Warren said in her letter to the USDA. "The index combines the more than $17.2 billion in rising grocery prices — calculated by inflation-adjusting consumer expenditures — with the more than $5.1 billion in lost household SNAP benefits."
The USDA and White House didn't return a request for comment.

Changing SNAP policies would require lawmakers to pass new rules for the food-stamp program. Some anti-hunger advocates and state organizations are now lobbying Congress to delay some of the OBBBA's changes to SNAP, including a rule that would require states with high payment error rates to absorb billions in additional costs starting in October 2027.

The USDA serves as the primary federal regulator and rule-maker for SNAP, giving it some leeway in administering the program. For instance, the agency allowed some states to ban enrollees from using food stamps to buy soda and candy, although a federal judge earlier this year ruled that the Agriculture Department exceeded its authority in implementing the rules.

Warren also pointed to President Trump's tariffs as contributing to higher food prices. Higher import duties last year boosted U.S. inflation by about 2.9 percentage points through February, according to recent research from the New York Fed. Without those tariffs, the price of goods would have declined, the researchers said.

title: This teacherless school says AI can teach students in 2 hours a day
summary: Alpha Schools says its AI-based instruction and focus on developing "life skills" set students up for success. Some experts say it's too good to be true.
story: Zane Shah arrives at school at 8:45 a.m., greets his friends and stores his backpack in the assigned cubby. It could be any middle school morning. But one thing about Shah's school is different: There are no traditional teachers.

Shah, 13, is an eighth grader at Alpha School, a network of private, for-profit institutions that opened its first Chicago campus this fall for students in pre-K through eighth grade. The adults in the building are called "guides," and artificial intelligence handles all the academic instruction.

When school starts at 9 a.m., students work on math, reading, writing, language and science on laptops, using adaptive software that Alpha says lets them master core subjects in roughly two hours a day.
That mastery doesn't come cheap. Attending Alpha Chicago costs $55,000 a year, or roughly $8,000 more than the average annual cost of a private college, according to U.S. News & World Report.

Alpha was founded in Austin, Texas, in 2014 by MacKenzie Price, who has become an outspoken critic of traditional schooling. Alpha says its students score in the top 1% on national standardized tests. The school also says it does not screen applicants based on previous grades or test scores. Instead, they look for students who are coachable, self-motivated and open to the learning model.
The school says students are only asked to leave for behavioral issues, not failure to meet academic standards.

"They're getting accepted to fantastic schools — Stanford, Northwestern, Rice," said Brian Howell, dean of parents at Alpha Chicago and formerly an anthropology professor at Wheaton College in Illinois.

Shah, who started at Alpha this year, previously attended traditional schools. Two hours of daily academic instruction is enough to accomplish everything he had learned in a typical eight-hour school day, he told CBS News.
"I feel like I can be more focused instead of having 20 to 30 kids in a classroom all talking at once," Shah said.
"Not interacting with chatbots"

Learning at Alpha centers on the school's proprietary educational software, which is used across all of Alpha's campuses and at a handful of affiliated private schools. The system, called TimeBack, was developed by a research team led by cognitive scientist Carl Hendrick of the Netherlands' Academica University of Applied Sciences.

TimeBack is designed to adjust to students' individual skills and capabilities over the course of the school year. For example, if a student repeatedly errs in tackling the same type of problem, the software returns to earlier concepts to fill in any knowledge gaps, according to Alpha.

Alpha also relies on a learning science team comprising subject-matter experts based globally, including licensed teachers, curriculum experts or specialists in early childhood education. They review student data daily, tracking each child's progress and whether they've met their academic goals. The team also builds the curriculum and steps in through remote coaching calls as a last resort if students bog down and need additional help.

Alpha says their approach works more like a private tutor than a chatbot because the software doesn't provide answers; instead, the system is designed to test students' knowledge until it determines they've properly learned a given lesson. The technology is also "closed," meaning it doesn't draw on information from the open internet.
"It's important to understand that they're not interacting with chatbots. They're not getting answers from AI," Howell said.
Replacing teachers with "guides"

Another unusual aspect of Alpha schools is that most guides don't have a background in education. A February analysis from the University of Colorado's National Education Policy Center, a nonpartisan think tank, reported that only about one-third of Alpha guides have education training or degrees.
Carrington Haas, Alpha Chicago's lead guide, told CBS News that staffers at the schools play a different role than traditional teachers.
"We're not teaching academics. The main part of our job is to support the students motivationally and emotionally," she said.
Asked whether guides answer academic questions, Haas added, "No, the academics team has their support so they can jump on a coaching call."
Yet Haas, who has a background in traditional education, including stints at Teach For America and at a Waldorf charter school, rejected the idea that the school is teacherless.
"I think it's the future," she said. "And it's not teacherless because we're still there and we're still very much teaching the life skills that they need to know."

Howell described Alpha's approach as mastery-based, meaning students don't advance until they've demonstrated understanding of a concept. When a student gets stuck, the guide doesn't immediately offer help; instead, it directs the student to reread the problem while drawing on hints from the adaptive software.
"Human beings are looking at those data. They're looking at the dashboards. They're seeing where are students getting stuck, where are they going faster?" Howell said.
Despite Alpha centering its pedagogy on computer-mediated learning, Howell also dismisses any notion that the school's educational approach amounts to parking kids in front of a screen.

"It is not just some mind-numbing, screen-based, zombifying project," he told CBS News. "The AI is not making any decisions about what students learn. The AI's not in control of a student's day — humans are."
So far, Binoy Shah is encouraged by his son's early experience, noting that he quickly noticed a change in Zane's engagement with his education.

"As a 13-year-old kid before you'd get, how was school? Good. How was your lunch? Good. What did you do today? Nothing," Binoy said. "Now we're getting three to five minutes of conversation [about] what he did at school, and he's excited about it."
Experts question Alpha's approach
For all the hype around artificial intelligence, education experts aren't sold on Alpha's unconventional teaching methods and AI-delivered curriculum.

While affirming the value of teaching life skills, such as communication and leadership, Rebecca Winthrop, a senior fellow at the nonpartisan Brookings Institution who has visited Alpha's campuses, questions the school's claims about its educational approach and outcomes. She also urges families who are interested in the school to ensure they know what they're signing up for.
"Parents should know that this is an experimental model. There's no clear externally validated evidence around the results they claim," she said.
"Neuroscience says that deep reflection — meaning-making, which a lot of times schools don't allow enough time for —  is really important for learning and long-term student outcomes," Winthrop added.
Other experts are more bluntly critical of Alpha's approach, accusing the school network of effectively financializing education.

"Alpha School is less an effort to expand educational opportunity than an experiment in extracting maximum profit from schooling," said Carol Corbett Burris, executive director of the Network for Public Education, a nonprofit advocacy group that supports public education.

Burris said Alpha's founders implemented its model at Unbound Academy, a free public charter school in Arizona, built on its TimeBack learning platform. She told CBS News the institution performed "dismally" when compared to Arizona's public schools, "despite the promises submitted in its charter application."
