title: Trump says new fuel supply push will lower prices. Will it work?
summary: The Trump administration said using the DPA funding will increase refining output and lower fuel prices for Americans. Experts are skeptical.
story: President Trump on Thursday said his administration will invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production in the U.S., the latest effort from the administration to lower fuel prices.

The Defense Production Act, or DPA, is a Korean War-era law that allows the president to use loans, purchase commitments and other mechanisms to incentivize the production of critical materials and goods.
The announcement follows a meeting President Trump had with refiners to discuss immediate steps to bring more capacity online, a White House official told CBS News.

In a press release on Thursday, the Department of Energy said the DPA funding will increase U.S. refining output by millions of gallons per day and lower fuel prices for Americans, who have been paying more than $4 a gallon on average for gas over the last three months.

The new plan to increase fuel production comes as polling shows a majority of Americans are pessimistic about the U.S. economy amid a growing affordability crunch. Crude oil prices have continued to climb, hitting their highest level this week since May.
On Friday, Brent crude, the international standard, was $116 a barrel, up 2.6%, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was around $103 a barrel, up 3%.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline stood at $4.29 on Friday and $6.32 for diesel, according to AAA. Those prices represent a 40% and 74% jump from a year earlier, respectively.

Passed in 1950, the DPA was originally aimed at boosting supplies for national defense purposes. However, Congress has broadened its application to address natural hazards, terrorist attacks and other national emergencies.
Will the measure be effective?
Experts told CBS News that invoking the DPA is unlikely to do much to lower fuel prices.
"I don't think that's really going to have any impact," Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at GasBuddy, told CBS News in an email.

There are some potential upsides: DPA funds could speed up some refining expansions, Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, told CBS News. However, he said any short-term benefits are unlikely.
"There is no slack in U.S. refining, so production can't be added regardless of political will," Kloza said. He said it typically takes months and calendar quarters to bring units back to service.
The White House official said the DFA funds will help expand capacity and modernize existing infrastructure, which is much faster than building a new refinery.
The U.S. produces more fuel than it consumes. Oil prices, however, are set on the global market, where the Iran war and Russia-Ukraine conflict have disrupted shipments, pushing prices higher.

The U.S. produces around 5.3 million barrels of distillate fuel oil, a category that includes diesel, per day but consumes only about 3.6 million barrels per day, experts have noted. The U.S. also produces 9.5 million barrels of gasoline per day, more than the 8.9 million consumed domestically.
The U.S. exports about 1.4 million barrels of diesel per day, Kloza, told CBS News.
A spokesperson for the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers, a trade association that represents refiners, said it appreciated the Trump administration's focus on the importance of refineries.

"Our country's 128 operating refineries produce more fuel in the United States than we consume," the spokesperson said in an email. "They are running all-out to keep Americans supplied and the global economy moving despite major disruptions and actual fuel shortages in other parts of the world."

title: Buttigieg endorses independent Seth Bodnar in Montana Senate race
summary: Pete Buttigieg chose to endorse independent Seth Bodnar over the Democratic Senate nominee, Alani Bankhead. Bodnar says he will not caucus with Democrats if he wins.
story: Former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg has endorsed the independent candidate in the Montana Senate race, Seth Bodnar, over the Democratic nominee, Bodnar's campaign announced Friday.

"The best leaders I've served with, in uniform and in government, care more about getting the job done than about who gets the credit, and Seth is one of them," Buttigieg, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said in a statement. "Seth and I don't agree on everything, but he has spent his adult life serving this country and the next generation, from the Army Green Berets to the University of Montana, and he'll bring that same character to the Senate on behalf of all Montanans."
Bodnar said he was "honored to have Secretary Buttigieg's support, and proud that people across the political spectrum are joining this campaign."

He says that if he's elected senator, he will not caucus with Democrats or Republicans, remaining independent. Bodnar, 47, a retired U.S. Army Green Beret who graduated first in his West Point class, is a Rhodes scholar and was until recently the president of the University of Montana. He's running against Democratic nominee Alani Bankhead and Republican nominee Kurt Alme.

Montana is considered a solidly GOP state, with far more voters who have cast ballots for Republican candidates than Democrats. Bodnar's resume and platform of independence, affordability and fighting corruption appear to be winning some support with Montanans, and as a result, Bankhead has faced calls to drop out of the race to give him a better shot at victory. With both on the ballot, they are likely to split the support of those who are not voting for Alme.
Republican Sen. Steve Daines' abrupt decision to not seek reelection shortly before the March filing deadline opened the vacancy.

President Trump held a rally in Montana last week to get out the vote for both Alme and congressional candidate Aaron Flint. Vice President JD Vance is also expected to hold a rally in Montana next week.

Nikole  Killion
                  
        contributed to this report.

title: House hunter discovers deceased body in vacant home
summary: In an exclusive interview, a homebuyer shares vivid details of finding a dead man during a house tour.
story: Florida resident David Hammersley and his family were fleeing from the hurricanes that plagued Florida and decided to tour homes in Kentucky. While house hunting on Sept. 26, 2022, their realtor showed them a rural 2-acre lot with a main house, a detached garage, and a cottage in Burkesville, Kentucky — a town known as the fishing capital of Kentucky.

"The house was immaculate. No furnishings in it. You can eat off the floor," Hammersley told correspondent Peter Van Sant in "The Mansion Above Dale Hollow Lake," an all-new "48 Hours" airing Saturday at 10/9c on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.
Hammersley was impressed with the property, including the sight of a Dodge truck found inside the detached garage.
"And I started to salivate over the possibility of that being part of the deal," he said.
As Hammersley and his family approached the cottage at the far end of the property, they were overpowered by a stench radiating from the cottage.
"It had to be something like a dead raccoon, in my opinion," Hammersley said.
Hammersley and his father-in-law proceeded to investigate, and within moments they stumbled across a horrific scene.
"I saw a man on the floor, his arm outstretched, obviously dead, from gunshot wounds," Hammersley told Van Sant.

They immediately contacted the authorities, who identified that man as Michael "Mike" Harding, a California transplant who resided across the Kentucky border in Tennessee. He had been missing for over a week.

An autopsy revealed that Harding had been shot four times — twice in the head and twice in the torso. Authorities found his phone at the crime scene and lead investigator BJ Burton from the Kentucky State Police examined it to see if it could answer their questions.
"Once you start looking through the text messages and phone calls, it becomes very obvious early on that he was lured to the house," Burton told Van Sant.

Investigators learned Harding had been contacted by a realtor named James Fraser requesting a repair service because Harding worked as an HVAC technician. However, they discovered the number used to contact Harding came from a prepaid cellphone.
"It was pretty evident early on that this is a burner phone," Burton said.

Burton also discovered Harding was going through a contentious divorce with his wife Julie Harding, a captain with the California Highway Patrol. The two were living in separate places — he was in Tennessee and she was in California.

"I feel like he was blinded by love. He truly loved her ... So, I thought he found his dream girl. But to me personally, I just, I didn't like her," Mike Harding's daughter, Heather Cavalieri, told "48 Hours."

Friends and family of Mike Harding told authorities he feared Julie Harding. They got access to her call log and learned that in the months leading up to his murder, Julie Harding had around 194 calls with a man from Houston. His name was Thomas O'Donnell and he was a former car salesman now living in Napa, California.
They also determined that the prepaid phone and O'Donnell's phone were located together a few weeks before Mike Harding's death.

"And the first thing you notice is ... the phone is first turned on when it's in the Houston, Texas, area," Burton said. "I don't think Mr. O'Donnell got out here by accident. The only connection that he had to Michael Harding was through Julie Harding."

On Dec. 8, 2022, just two months after Mike Harding was found dead, authorities arrested O'Donnell for his murder. For Julie Harding, two days after O'Donnell's arrest, she was found dead at the Tennessee home where Mike Harding had been living. An investigator determined she had died by suicide.

Burton believes Julie Harding may have feared she would lose hundreds of thousands of dollars in their divorce, so she conspired with O'Donnell to kill her estranged husband. O'Donnell pleaded not guilty to the murder charge and would face trial three years after his arrest. A Kentucky jury found him guilty, and he was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 20 years.

title: Trump administration to push for new labels on seafood
summary: The Trump administration intends to push for new labels on seafood sold at grocery stores to give consumers a better idea of where products originated.
story: The Trump administration intends to push for new labels on seafood sold at grocery stores to give consumers a better idea of where products originated, two U.S. officials told CBS News.
However, the "U.S. Caught Seafood" label, proposed by the Food and Drug Administration, wouldn't be mandatory.

President Trump was expected to mention seafood during his pitch to voters in Florida on Friday afternoon. He is stumping in Fort Myers for Senate candidate Ashley Moody and gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds before spending the night at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Palm Beach.
The White House has prepared economy-related perks to roll out in each of the states he visits in the final campaign blitz before the midterm elections.

Most seafood eaten in the U.S. is imported, government data shows. About 80% of the seafood Americans ate in 2023 came from abroad, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. U.S. commercial fishermen caught seafood valued at $5.1 billion in 2023, while the U.S. imported $25 billion worth.

The Trump administration was also preparing $5 billion in loans targeted at the fishing industry so that it can buy new equipment, according to U.S. officials. The loans would be through the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
This story published first on CBS News at 12:08 p.m. on Oct. 23, 2026.

title: Trumps to vote early in person in Florida on Saturday
summary: President Trump and first lady Melania Trump are expected to vote early in Palm Beach County.
story: President Trump and first lady Melania Trump will vote early in person in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Saturday, a White House official said.
On the campaign trail this week, the president said he prefers to vote on Election Day. But Mr. Trump is registered to vote in Palm Beach County.
In recent elections, Mr. Trump has voted by mail. The president, however, is critical of widespread mail-in voting.
Saturday is the first day of early voting in Florida, which runs from Oct. 24 through Halloween.
Mr. Trump's Election Day plans are not yet clear. He didn't answer when reporters asked this week what he'll be doing that day.

The president is traveling most days to hold rallies for Republicans. He was in South Carolina Wednesday night and in Iowa Thursday night, and will deliver remarks in Fort Meyers, Florida, Friday before heading to Mar-a-Lago.

title: Anthropic previews Claude Duet personal AI agent for subscribers
summary: Anthropic said Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for paying subscribers. Here's what it can do.
story: Anthropic has joined the race to develop AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of humans with Claude Duet, a new app it previewed this week.
The agent competes with Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots, rival developers' agents that are already popular with consumers.
Claude Duet is only available by waitlist as a research preview for Claude U.S. Pro and Max subscribers, according to Anthropic.
What can Claude Duet do?
Claude Duet works as a "proactive agent" for human customers, taking autonomous actions to complete tasks assigned to it.

"It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away and checks with you before it acts on your behalf," Anthropic said, noting that it was designed for professionals and small business owners "with more on their plates than they can track."
Anthropic said Claude Duet's utility lies in its superior judgment, describing it as smart enough to know what to prioritize and which tasks require a user's attention.

Each morning, Claude Duet sends its user a daily brief outlining the day's most important items. For the agent to have context, it must be connected to a person's apps, like their email accounts and calendars. Some security professionals have raised concerns about new AI agents' access to such information, warning users to limit how much they share.
"Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work," Anthropic said.
What about security issues?
Anthropic highlighted built-in security measures that it says make the app safe to use, noting that the agent never directly sees a person's passwords or sign-in tokens.

Claude Duet can also handle administrative tasks like scheduling meetings and creating financial or sales forecasts. It can build web apps, too, Anthropic said. It can draft job postings or make purchases on a business owner's behalf.
Anthropic researchers who have tested the app have used it to manage their to-do lists, build apps, schedule interviews and more.
How do you sign up?
Anthropic said people can sign up on the waitlist at its Claude Duet product page.
Invitations are issued in waves, and the product is only available in the U.S. during its research preview, the company said.
"We're adding people gradually, and you'll get an email when it's your turn," the company said.

title: 2 pilots eject from military training jet in Texas after landing gear issue
summary: The pilots were aboard a T-6A Texan II assigned to the 12th Flying Training Wing when they ejected from the aircraft.
story: Two pilots safely ejected from a military training aircraft near Seguin, Texas, on Thursday after experiencing a landing gear issue, officials said.

The pilots were aboard a T-6A Texan II assigned to the 12th Flying Training Wing when they conducted a "controlled bailout" at approximately 5:51 p.m. local time, according to a news release from Joint Base San Antonio.
After receiving indications that the aircraft's landing gear was unsafe, the pilots consulted experts, who recommended they eject, officials said.
Both pilots were being evaluated by local medical personnel. Their conditions were not immediately known.
The T-6A Texan II is a single-engine, two-seat primary trainer designed to train students in basic flying skills for U.S. Air Force and Navy pilots, according to the U.S. Air Force.

The 12th Flying Training Wing "develops the next generation of Air Force aviators and enlisted aircrew by providing world-class flying training and education," according to the Air Education and Training Command.
Seguin is located about 35 miles east of San Antonio.

title: More people now use GLP-1s to lose weight than for other health issues
summary: Growing usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss is reshaping how consumers shop for food and clothes, according to consulting firm EY-Parthenon.
story: More Americans are now taking GLP-1 drugs to shed some pounds than to treat diabetes and other health conditions for which the medications were originally prescribed, new research shows.
Roughly 54% of people taking semaglutide medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy do so to lose weight, overtaking the share of people who use them for other medical reasons, according to EY-Parthenon.

Meanwhile, as usage of GLP-1 drugs for weight management surpasses other medical uses, more consumers are changing how they eat and shop, the strategy consulting firm found in a survey of nearly 15,000 people, including 3,602 current or former GLP-1 users.

For example, people taking the drugs typically consume fewer unhealthy foods and less alcohol in favor of healthier products. Sixty-three percent of GLP-1 users say they have reduced their consumption of sweet snacks, while 57% say they eat fewer salty snacks, according to EY-Parthenon's research.
Food makers, grocery chains and other retailers are adapting to those changes in consumer habits.

"We are finding that manufacturers and retailers are making more room on store shelves for GLP-1-diet-specific foods, or protein-enhanced items, and smaller portion sizes," Don Johnson, a principal in EY-Parthenon's consumer strategy practice, told CBS News. "Some consumer packaged goods makers thought this was a blip or fad. Now I don't hear that. Everyone accepts that this is a structural change that's not going away."
Smaller sizes, fitted styles

Growing use of the drugs for controlling weight is also changing how consumers shop for clothes. In the apparel department, EY-Parthenon researchers found that consumers taking GLP-1s are gravitating toward smaller clothing sizes and more fitted clothing, swimwear and athletic wear.
"You're losing a lot of weight on the drugs, so you're needing to buy differently," Johnson said.

EY-Parthenon found that 72% of GLP-1 users sized down in clothing after rapidly losing weight, requiring a wardrobe refresh. Roughly half of users increased their spending on fitness services, such as gym memberships, while 46% switched apparel brands.

GLP-1s have become accessible to a broader swath of consumers, driving increased adoption for weight loss, according to EY-Parthenon. The drugs are today available in more forms, such as a pill, and are also more affordable, leading more younger, lower-income and male consumers to use the drugs, according to the research.

Changes in public policy are also helping drive wider usage of the drugs. A Trump administration agreement last year with GLP-1 manufacturers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk lowered the cost of Ozempic and Wegovy to between $150 and $350 per month, down from roughly $1,000 per month. The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program also provides eligible Medicare beneficiaries with access to GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month.

GLP-1 drugs also could have clinical value in helping people deal with other issues, some researchers think. Experts at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania are embarking on a study to see if the drugs can deter risky financial decisions.

In a first-of-its-kind study, the researchers will examine how GLP-1s influence the body's reward system, a network of brain structures that reinforces certain behaviors, to see whether the drugs suppress temptations such as luxury purchases, gambling or other activities that people often find hard to control.

title: Trump praises Ramaswamy ad as some GOP critics speak out
summary: "Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" President Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"
story: Washington — President Trump on Thursday praised the "very powerful ad" Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is running featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, after the ad drew pushback from some Republicans like Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine.
Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that he suggested Ramaswamy keep the ad up, saying the press is "trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good!"

The ad, which first circulated on social media on Monday and is now television, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar" and sought to undermine her credibility. Acton's campaign condemned the ad, and her brother, Philip Stearns, called it a "despicable low."

According to court documents provided by the campaign, Arthur's now-deceased husband was charged with raping Acton, which she said occurred when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial.

DeWine on Thursday said he thought the Ramaswamy campaign should take the ad down. "It's wrong to run this ad," the Ohio Republican told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down." DeWine did not rescind his endorsement.
But Vice President JD Vance and now Mr. Trump are defending the ad and using it to criticize Acton.

"Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse," Mr. Trump wrote in his social media post. "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad.' Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
In his post, Mr. Trump did not mention why Acton and her birth mother are estranged, or any of the family's backstory.

Shortly after his post, on the White House South Lawn, reporters told Mr. Trump the backstory — that Acton's mother stayed married to the man charged with raping her. CBS News senior White House reporter Weijia Jiang asked the president why anyone should listen to what the estranged mother has to say.

"Well I know nothing about it," the president responded. "All I know is the mother said very bad things about Acton, who I guess is running for governor against Vivek. And all I can say is Vivek is great. And I know one thing, if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story, that's for sure. So I don't know what it is, but I guess the mother said very bad things about the one who's running for governor. And I think you have to say that seriously."
"I'm defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it, you would love every inch of it," Mr. Trump added.
In his Truth Social post, the president specifically went after DeWine.

"Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party," Mr. Trump wrote. "He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up..."
Mr. Trump added he only wishes the "mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse."
"Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" Mr. Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"

Mr. Trump continued to defend the ad during a rally in Iowa late Thursday. He said he advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it," later adding: "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much.'"
Vance, too, defended the ad, saying Republicans who have criticized it should "stop whining."
Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, who is running for reelection, said he "would not have run that ad."
Outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina called the ad the "most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season."
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told a local ABC station he "probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."

Acton's brother said earlier this week it's "not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point."

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

title: More parents facing charges for their children's e-motorcycle crashes
summary: Among those charged were the mother and father of 13-year-old Benson Nguyen, who died after crashing his e-moto into a light pole in Southern California.
story: Parents in a growing number of communities are being held responsible by authorities when their children are involved in serious accidents involving electric motorcycles.
Videos of the practice often emerge on social media showing groups of children illegally riding e-motos, often performing dangerous stunts on busy roads.
In California, it is illegal for children under 16 to ride e-motos, which have a higher-powered motor than electric bikes.

In Southern California, Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer has attempted to crack down on the growing problem, bringing charges this year against 12 parents who are accused of letting their children illegally ride e-motos.
"I need to send a message in order to save other kids' lives and to make sure other parents are taking responsibility for their children," Spitzer told CBS News.
Among those charged were the mother and father of 13-year-old Benson Nguyen, who had posted videos of himself to his TikTok channel doing risky tricks.

In May, police said Nguyen was driving his e-moto recklessly at more than 40 miles per hour in the Orange County city of Garden Grove when he lost control and crashed into a light pole. He was taken to an area hospital, where he died from his injuries. Nguyen's parents were charged with child endangerment.
Spitzer said he does not want to prosecute parents, but feels he has to.
"I am a human being. I've raised two kids," Spitzer said. "We have to understand that when you break the law, especially as serious as this is, there has to be consequences."
According to numbers from the Orange County DA, there have been more than 125 deaths and tens of thousands of injuries attributed to e-bikes and e-motos across the U.S.
In Orange County, they are now the leading cause of juvenile emergency room visits, the DA's office said.
"You shouldn't furnish your kid a gun not understanding what they might do with that weapon," Spitzer said. "And you certainly shouldn't furnish a vehicle like an e-bike or an e-motorcycle."

title: Supreme Court rules New Hampshire can ban use of student IDs for voters
summary: The Supreme Court cleared the way Thursday for New Hampshire to fully ban the use of student IDs for voting during the midterm elections.
story: The Supreme Court cleared the way Thursday for New Hampshire to fully ban the use of student IDs for voting during the midterm elections.
The justices granted a Republican-backed emergency appeal and blocked the use of student IDs as a backup method of identification.

New Hampshire passed a law this year that said student IDs would no longer be an expressly accepted form of identification for obtaining a ballot. The secretary of state then issued guidance barring them as a backup way to prove a voter's identity.
A judge left the law in place but blocked the guidance in early October, prompting the appeal to the Supreme Court. The Republican National Committee weighed in to support the state.

In its brief one-paragraph decision, the Supreme Court invoked the longstanding "Purcell principle," quoting a previous 2020 decision that stated that the high court "has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election."
The decision was unsigned. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent from the ruling, arguing that the Purcell principle did not necessarily apply in this case.

"It seems to me that a case involving a court order like the one at issue here—which left the state election rule untouched—does not necessarily fall within the ambit of Purcell and its concern about federal courts 'changing the election rules' at the last minute," Jackson wrote.
The Supreme Court wrote in its opinion Thursday that the lower court "did not point to anything that would justify deviating" from the Purcell principle.

In a statement, Republican New Hampshire Attorney General John Formella praised the ruling, writing that "New Hampshire has a responsibility to protect the integrity of its elections and ensure that election laws are applied as written."
Formella called it "an important victory for our efforts to defend those laws and prevent last-minute court orders from creating uncertainty for voters and election officials."
The decision comes less than two weeks before New Hampshire voters cast ballots in a closely contested U.S. Senate race.

title: Judge says Trump must sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit
summary: A federal judge said President Trump must sit for a deposition with lawyers for the BBC by Dec. 11 as part of his ongoing defamation lawsuit.
story: Washington — A federal judge said President Trump must sit for a deposition with lawyers for the BBC by Dec. 11 as part of his ongoing defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett set the deadline during a hearing in Miami on Thursday morning, according to the Associated Press. The judge ordered Mr. Trump to answer questions by Dec. 11 or face penalties, which could include dismissal of his lawsuit against the BBC, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended, the AP reported.

Mr. Trump was supposed to sit for a deposition Friday, but his lawyers told the BBC late last month that he would no longer be available to answer questions "due to other matters of national importance." The BBC told the court that on the day of the scheduled deposition, Oct. 16, the president spoke at a rally in Georgia alongside GOP candidates for the Senate and governor. He then traveled to his South Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago, where he attended an event for the Republican National Committee.
The president said he would be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
Lawyers for the broadcaster had asked the judge to compel Mr. Trump to confirm a date for the deposition and answer their questions.

In a statement, a spokesman for the president's legal team did not address the judge's demand for a deposition, but said his "powerhouse lawsuit is holding the BBC accountable for its defamation and reckless election interference just as he has held other fake news mainstream media responsible for their wrongdoing."

Mr. Trump filed his $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC in December over a documentary that featured spliced-together portions of a speech he gave outside the White House on Jan. 6, 2021. Mr. Trump alleged that the documentary, which aired in October 2024, just weeks before the presidential election, misled viewers and falsely depicted his remarks to supporters.

Following the president's speech, a crowd of his backers marched to the U.S. Capitol and breached the building, where lawmakers and then-Vice President Mike Pence were gathered to reaffirm the results of the 2020 election.

The BBC said in November 2025 that it "sincerely regrets" how the clip of Mr. Trump's speech was edited but disagreed that there was a basis for a defamation claim. The network apologized to the president.

At the hearing Thursday, lawyers for the BBC and the president were set to discuss the network's subpoena for deposition testimony from Jack Smith, the former special counsel who brought criminal charges against Mr. Trump in 2023. The case involved Mr. Trump's alleged efforts to subvert the transfer of presidential power after the 2020 election. The charges were dismissed after the president was elected to a second term in 2024.

In defending the subpoena for Smith's testimony, the BBC said in a court filing that the former special counsel could shed light on matters involving Mr. Trump's speech on Jan. 6, including whether the president knew his remarks could lead to violence. The network said Smith does not object to the subpoena.

But Mr. Trump's lawyers refuted the notion that Smith has personal knowledge about the president's speech or state of mind when he delivered it. They also said Smith's testimony would be "duplicative," since he authored a final report on his investigation and testified twice to Congress about his case against Mr. Trump.
The BBC is also seeking documents from Mar-a-Lago about its membership and initiation fees, which the president's lawyers argue does not serve a legitimate purpose.

The discovery process began in February and is set to end Dec. 18. BBC lawyers said in a filing that nearly eight months into discovery, they still have not spoken with Mr. Trump and do not have a schedule to question him. They called the president "the most central figure in this case."

"There is hardly a more crucial and relevant piece of discovery in a defamation lawsuit than the deposition of the Plaintiff. For that reason, a plaintiff's unwillingness to sit for a deposition can be perilous to his claim," they wrote in a motion earlier this month.

title: Roller coaster safety experts weigh in on Six Flags investigation
summary: The Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia has been closed since a man died after witnesses say he was ejected from the ride.
story: Ride inspection experts expect the investigation into the death of a man who fell from a Georgia roller coaster this month to examine if maintenance issues, design flaws or human error led to the incident at Six Flags Over Georgia.
The Goliath has been closed since 42-year-old Hassan Kariem died after witnesses say he was ejected from the ride.

John F. King, Georgia's Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, who is leading the investigation, said investigators will not "cut corners, rush to conclusions, or leave questions unanswered without making every effort to resolve them."
"Our team has been on the ground working day and night to ensure that every relevant detail receives the attention it deserves," he said in a statement last week.
A spokesperson for the park said in a statement to CBS News that "our thoughts remain with the family and loved ones affected by the tragic incident in Georgia."

"Nothing is more important to Six Flags than the safety of our guests and team members, and we remain focused on supporting ongoing investigations alongside state authorities and the ride manufacturer," the spokesperson said.

A March inspection of the Goliath roller coaster found no violations or deficiencies, King said. The inspection report did include a note indicating that staff "need to replace bushings" — a piece of the puzzle inspectors are sure to home in on, experts said.
Bushings are parts designed to reduce friction and absorb shock in various mechanical assemblies.
Maintenance issues or a design flaw?

Six Flags has opened five Goliath roller coasters at parks across North America in the last 25 years. The coaster, which opened in 2006 in Georgia, can reach speeds of up to 70 miles per hour on towering tracks that rise 200 feet. It was designed by Bolliger & Mabillard, a Swiss-based roller coaster manufacturer.

For Kariem to have been ejected from the ride, ride operators and roller coaster engineers suggested either a mechanical malfunction, operator error — for instance, failing to properly check and secure the restraint — or a combination of both, could have played a part. Rides and their restraints are supposed to be inspected by park maintenance each morning, they said.
The park spokesperson said, "Safety is our ethos and is at the heart of everything we do at Six Flags."

"Every ride undergoes documented safety inspections before opening each day, supported by comprehensive maintenance programs designed to meet or exceed industry safety guidelines," the spokesperson said. "Our ride operators complete a comprehensive, multi-stage training program that includes classroom instruction, hands-on training and supervised, on-the-job experience with additional instruction and evaluation provided whenever necessary."

When riders board the Goliath, they are buckled into the ride's 36 seats using a padded clamshell lap bar, a U-shaped restraint that is typically locked in place over a rider's thighs and waist. Ride operators check restraints to make sure they're locked before the ride begins.

Daniel, a self-described "big roller coaster nerd" who also operates a Goliath at another park, said the coaster is designed so staff can use a control panel with various buttons and a screen to operate the ride.

Daniel, who asked to use his middle name because he is still employed, said it was likely that ride operators used two orange buttons on the control panel to open and close the car restraints. When the sensors detect that every single restraint is closed, two green mushroom-shaped buttons at the bottom start blinking. That means that operators can press on them to dispatch the ride, he said.
Goliath inspection records obtained by CBS News, dating back over a decade, show a smattering of 20 quickly resolved violations between 2016 and 2021, and none since.
However, Troy Richardson, an engineer with experience building and inspecting roller coasters, said the March inspection's note about bushings could be significant.
Bushings are used to keep mechanical pieces in restraints, chassis joints and wheel bogies, positioned correctly amid the repeated friction and bumps of a roller coaster ride.
Even a small defect in a bushing can be a major problem, said Richardson, the founder and CEO of MIT Experts, which provides forensic consulting in amusement park litigation.
"A bushing, if it's slightly off a little bit, now the pin won't go into the hole or it's a little bit loose in the hole," he said.

Richardson added that the manufacturer of the roller coaster most likely laid out a maintenance and replacement schedule for each part in an operation manual. A key question investigators will ask, Richardson said, will be if staff adhered to those instructions.

A person with knowledge of the park's operations said the bushings identified in the March inspection were located on the ride's bogie assemblies, which connect the vehicle to the track, and unrelated to the restraint system. They were changed as recommended, the person said.
Another expert, Kathryn Woodcock, editor-in-chief of the Journal of Themed Experience and Attractions Studies, said investigators will want to know "what exactly is not the way it is expected to be."
"If two parts disconnected (e.g., a latch came undone), it is a different thing than if one part broke (e.g., a crack failed catastrophically)," Woodcock said.
Woodcock described the tricky process behind determining when to replace parts.
"It is not automatically better to replace a part too early," Woodcock, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, wrote in an email.

She said the likelihood of failure in roller coaster parts often falls along a "'bathtub curve,' where failure is most common at the start of use due to possible manufacturing defects, and then if it does not fail then, the failure likelihood is very low for a length of time — which depends on its material and shape and loading — when failure likelihood increases again."
"In charge of some very important systems"
Six Flags operates nearly three dozen parks across North America, with more than 47 million guests and 95,000 employees in 2025, according to SEC filings.

At Six Flags Magic Mountain in California, the death of 22-year-old Christopher Hawley after he rode the X2 roller coaster in 2022 prompted questions about ride maintenance and inspection, said Timothy Loranger, an attorney who represented Hawley's family.

"What I did see in having talked to people who maintained the rides, I did not come away from those conversations feeling confident that they were competent in their jobs, I felt like they didn't have appropriate training," Loranger said. "They were in charge of some very important systems and maybe didn't really even understand what they were doing."

Six Flags Magic Mountain settled the wrongful death lawsuit with Hawley's family. The park shuttered X2 permanently in September, after lawsuits alleging riders suffered brain injuries piled up. (The Doan Law Firm, which tracks published claims of theme park-related fatalities, lists two previous deaths on Goliaths in its database: a 2002 brain aneurysm at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California and a 2006 death listed as a likely heart attack on Six Flags Over Georgia's Goliath.)
Loranger said he wouldn't be surprised if the same challenges he saw at Magic Mountain arose at Six Flags Over Georgia.
Ride operators at Six Flags Over Georgia spoke to CBS News about the training and management they received while being tasked with ensuring the safety of thrill-seekers.

Jacobi Edwards, 18, who was a ride operations lead at Six Flags Over Georgia for several months last spring, described it as "a very well-run place," saying he's proud of his work there. But he chose to work on other roller coasters, in part because of Goliath's popularity.
"They have a clock to beat as that is the most famous ride in the park, so they do definitely feel rushed," said Edwards, who was 17 when he worked at the park.
He said when he was on the clock, he prioritized guest safety over trying to get "more cycles in."
Richardson, the MIT engineer, said park supervisors need to trust park staff as "ambassadors … that are trying to keep people safe and be your frontline."

"I don't care if there's 100 people in the line, we don't want somebody to die, you know? And they need to have that ability to come in and say, 'Hey, I have the authority to shut this down if I don't think it's safe,'" Richardson said.
Richard Pretlow, park president of Six Flags Over Georgia, said in a statement after the incident, "our team members receive extensive training to safely operate and maintain our rides."

But Harper Henderson,18, a former employee who started her job at Six Flags Over Georgia when she was 15, said the pressure to keep lines for the Goliath moving was paralleled by the rush to get new employees trained to operate the coaster.
Like Edwards, Henderson said she was promoted to trainer at 17 years old — after six weeks as a ride operator.

"Whenever we got a new employee, I would walk them through the operating procedures for all the rides and then watch them as they pretend they're operating the ride, or pretend to help with the restraints or something," she said. "And I would do that over and over again until I thought they were ready for the test and then I would send them to take the test."
She described it as a process that "could be done in about an hour." Henderson said ride operators needed at least an hour to review all the training.

CBS News reviewed operator tests for two Six Flags Over Georgia rides: Georgia Scorcher and the Log Jamboree. The questions, on a Microsoft Forms sheet, asked about the mechanics of each ride and its safety procedures. For example, in the Georgia Scorcher quiz, operators are asked, "What does it mean when the DISPATCH buttons flash on the main operator?"
Henderson said the rides were often so busy she had to rush the training.
"We would just give them the test answers," Henderson said, adding that new operators would then be ready to work in "15 minutes."
Henderson said she wasn't comfortable with the process. She said she resigned in July 2025.
"The fact that you could just skip, that was not great," she said. "And it was because the managers really pushed to have the minimum amount of people to open every ride."

title: Hero bystander, teacher praised for saving lives in school shooting
summary: The bystander who pursued and killed the Silver Rail Elementary School shooter is thanking first responders and the community for their support.
story: The bystander who stepped in to stop a gunman at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, has come forward and identified himself as Kaylub Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident who has two daughters at the school. At a news conference Friday, police also praised a teacher who threw a cellphone at the gunman, tackled him and fought to take his weapon.
Police said Giamanco pursued and fatally shot the 16-year-old attacker, ending a rampage that took the lives of three children and a teacher and wounded two others.

A statement released by Giamanco's family on Friday said, "He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support."
"The tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary has devastated the Bend community," they wrote.
Giamanco and his family asked for privacy and said they will not be giving interviews.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz credited him and a teacher at the school for actions that saved other lives.

"In addition to the 36-year-old man who bravely stepped in to stop the suspect, I want to highlight another person whose heroic action we need to recognize: a teacher in the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect and then tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him. She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," he said.
President Trump on Friday called the Giamanco a "great hero" who "took care of business."
"Thank God we had him; otherwise, it would have been much worse," Mr. Trump said, adding: "It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it."
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek also praised the bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life," saying the person's actions carry "a heavy emotional burden."
Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, says he called her shortly after it happened.

"Kaylub knew something was not right, so he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school," she said in an exclusive interview with CBS News Sacramento. "He crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army-crawled through the window."
She says he told her: "'A man went into my daughter's school and shot kids,' and he said, 'and I looked at him point-blank, and I shot and killed him, Mom.'"

"I told him he was a hero, he did what he had to do, and that he did the right thing, and that I was proud of him and that he was a hero and he saved a lot of lives," she said. "And he said, 'Mom, I couldn't save them all.' "
Freeman said, "Kaylub has a genuine heart and he loves his community and his family and his children," adding, "He's just a good person, in general."

When police arrived minutes later, Krantz says they found the deceased shooter and four victims — three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher — inside the school. Two other victims, a student and a teacher, were hospitalized with critical injuries.

At Friday's briefing, Krantz said the gunman has been identified as Griffin J. John II. He used a shotgun purchased by his mother, law enforcement sources told CBS News. The suspect was from Bend and had previously attended the school, police said.

title: Trump's U.N. envoy says Iran war could drag on for another year

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has told the Financial Times the war with Iran could last another year, but the Trump administration envoy said he hopes the Iranians "come to the table" before that. The price of Brent crude oil briefly crossed $117 a barrel Friday, its highest level during the war, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed to have disabled seven tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. President Trump accused Iran Thursday of lying about attacks on ships to drive up oil prices before the U.S. midterm elections. State-owned energy giant Saudi Aramco said Thursday that the amount of oil flowing through its East-West pipeline, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, had more than tripled from 2 million to 7 million barrels per day, as uncertainty hangs over exports across the Middle East.

title: Meghan "deeply distressed" as dad faces child abuse material probe
summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is facing a probe in the Philippines over alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: London — Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, said in a statement sent to CBS News Friday that she was "deeply distressed" by reports that her father, Thomas Markle, is under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.

Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said she had been aware of allegations against her father since 2018, and that those allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.

"In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," her Friday statement said.
At this time, it is understood that the Metropolitan Police has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle.

"We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018," a Metropolitan Police spokesperson said. "We are undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."
Meghan said she had distanced herself from her father in an effort to protect her children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

The British tabloid The Sun reported Thursday that Thomas Markle, who has been estranged from his daughter for years, had been reported to authorities in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr., after the younger man allegedly discovered child abuse materials in storage boxes at his father's home in the Philippines.
The Daily Mail reported Friday that Markle had denied the allegations against him.
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the newspaper, as well as dismissing the allegations as "sick lies."

According to the Mail, Thomas Jr. made the discovery while his father was in the United States being treated for a stroke and blood clot. The son initially saw some of the materials after turning on an old cell phone at his father's home in the Philippines, and he subsequently reported the materials in July to an FBI hotline, as well as the National Center for Exploited and Missing Children and state police in Pennsylvania, according to the newspaper's report.
Philippines state media confrimed Friday, in a post shared on Facebook, that an investigation was underway.

"The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday said it is investigating reports involving an octogenarian American national who left child abuse videos and photos in his home in Cebu province," the state-run Philippine News Agency said.

A Filipino justice official said the department's anti-trafficking task force was investigating the matter and it confirmed that Thomas Markle Sr. was the subject of the investigation, according to the PNA report.
Meghan said in her statement that her "sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children."

title: Gunmen kill at least 7 in attack on Jordan church, authorities say
summary: Jordan's King Abdullah II vowed the "harshest retaliation" after gunmen carried out a deadly attack on a church.
story: Gunmen carried out a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan during a funeral Friday, authorities said. At least seven people were killed in the shooting, the kingdom's interior minister said.

Mazen Al-Faraya said at a press conference that 34 other people were wounded in the rare attack on Christians in the majority Sunni Muslim kingdom. The interior minister said a group of extremists carried out the shooting.
Jordan's King Abdullah II vowed the "harshest retaliation" against the attackers.
"Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation," he said on social media.

Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate before opening fire, the public security directorate said in a statement. Karak, home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, is 110 miles south of the capital, Amman.
The gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession, the directorate added, saying a manhunt was underway for the perpetrators.

Footage aired by state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka showed the moment of the attack. In the video, two gunmen are seen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun, before they open fire on the church from an entrance on the street and charge forward.
Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.
An eyewitness told Al-Mamlaka that a vehicle arrived carrying the gunmen, who fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.
Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, the Arab world's only Christian head of state, called the shooting at the church a "heinous terrorist attack."
He said that it "reaffirms once again that terrorism has no religion and no homeland, and its aim is to strike at coexistence and spread strife," according to a presidency statement.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

title: Melania Trump secures "temporary ceasefire" in Ukrainian city
summary: First lady Melania Trump's office says she secured a localized ceasefire for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.
story: First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons.

In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.

Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement. But Ukrainian officials indicated that there has been a tentative agreement in the Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."

"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."

The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
The first lady added that she's secured an American media organization to document both Russian and Ukrainian teams. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, said it would be going.
White House communications director Steven Cheung called the announcement "amazing news."
"This is a major, positive step towards peace," Cheung said on X. "History will remember her tireless work to help those in need."
Last week, the Vatican said Pope Leo spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the phone and "expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky."
Melania Trump has worked to reunite 34 children so far with their families, after Russia forcibly removed children.

Although he said he would bring about an end to Russia's war with Ukraine on his first day back in office, peace has remained elusive for Mr. Trump. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, saying Ukraine should have a new leader and dismissing concerns about Russia's continued slaughter of Ukrainians.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this week. "They haven't been doing much."
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced backlash for calling Putin a "humanitarian" upon the release of American Stephen Hubbard.

title: Deadly shooting in Paris suburb may be terrorist act, officials say
summary: Officials said they are investigating a drive-by shooting in Trappes, outside Paris, as a potential terrorist act and called it a "miracle" that there weren't more casualties.
story: A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and wounded several others in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, authorities said, and prosecutors are investigating the case as a potential terrorist act. Officials say at least two of the victims were from immigrant backgrounds.
The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.

"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, The Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties.
Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.
The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.
Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.
A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.
Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."

Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.
They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"
A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.
Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."

Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.
France on edge after street violence and protests

The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.

French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.

Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.
Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the AP reported.

title: Kushner pushes back on report involving phone, spies, transfer
summary: An excerpt from an upcoming book claims Kushner had access to alleged Middle Eastern "slush" funds when he served as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration. Kushner and his legal team deny the accusations.
story: Jared Kushner is pushing back on a report involving a hacked iPhone, international spies and billion-dollar transfers from foreign governments.

An upcoming book by journalist Matthew Cole claims Kushner, who is President Trump's son-in-law, had access to more than $2 billion in "slush money funds" from Middle Eastern leaders in an attempt to influence U.S. foreign policy.

An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.

Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom.

The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."

An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.

According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."
At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.

The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.

According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.

The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."
Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."
"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.
CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.
Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."
"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

title: Delicate operation carried out on explosives-packed WWII shipwreck
summary: Engineers sprang into action amid concern that an 82-year-old WWII shipwreck's crumbling masts could topple and set off its 1,500-ton sunken explosives payload.
story: Sheerness, England — A delicate operation aimed at preventing an 82-year-old U.S. shipwreck packed with tons of World War II explosives from unleashing a potentially catastrophic tidal wave on London has been completed. But while the most imminent danger has been addressed, the explosives remain inside the rusting wreck of the SS Richard Montgomery on the riverbed, and experts aren't taking their eyes off it.

The Montgomery, one of about 2,700 Liberty ships built in the U.S. to support the Allied war effort, was grounded on a sandbar off the town of Sheerness in the Thames Estuary, just 40 miles from the British capital, in August 1944. It was carrying munitions intended to support the Allies following the D-Day landings.
The vessel broke apart during salvage efforts and sank, with an estimated 1,500 tons of explosives in its cargo holds.

The ship's three rusting masts protruding from the water had been a familiar sight to residents and passing vessels for decades. But recent surveys revealed increasing deterioration in the structure, raising fears the masts could collapse and trigger an explosion.

"The vessel was starting to lean and deteriorate, so they could see some of the structures around the mast starting to collapse," Nolan Conway, a naval architect with Florida-based marine salvage firm Resolve Marine Group, which was contracted to remove the masts, told CBS News.

"The fear is the masts could have fallen onto the cargo itself, causing it to detonate," he said. "Some of the munitions are believed to be fused munitions with pressure fuses, so something like an impact could potentially set them off."

U.K. maritime minister Keir Mather told lawmakers in the House of Commons this week that the "complex project requiring specialist program, engineering and risk management expertise" had been completed ahead of schedule and on budget, with all three of the masts removed at a cost of just under $13 million, according to The Guardian.
Mather said in the U.K. Parliament that the masts had put "significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site."
The government has long maintained an exclusion zone around the wreck, which is about 1.5 miles off the Sheerness coast.
Mather told lawmakers the wreck would "continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone."
Removing the remaining explosives would carry considerable risks, and the consequences of an explosion remain the subject of debate among experts.

"The impact of this wreck detonating is unpredictable," Conway said. "Estimates range from impacting the shoreline, to creating a tidal wave that could travel up the Thames, to a rather minor event that could potentially just close a nearby shipping channel. There's a large range of impacts, but none of them are really good."
Officials continue to assess the overall risk of an explosion as low, but the deteriorating condition of the masts prompted authorities to act.
Conway said the challenge for the firm was to devise a way to remove the masts without disturbing the sunken ship's hull and the perilous cargo inside, or putting the people doing the work at risk.

"How can you cut off that mast without vibrating or impacting the wreck?" he said. "We designed a custom lifting frame to safely pick it up without the mast swinging or swaying as we lifted it free of the wreck."
Engineers used a remotely operated underwater diamond-wire saw that clamps "around the mast with hydraulic arms and passes the saw through without getting divers in the water," Conway explained.
The removal of the masts marks the end of a distinctive chapter in the wreck's history. The masts, visible above the estuary since World War II, are expected to be preserved for public display.

Mather, the U.K. maritime minister, said the masts had been moved to a local museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, and would be displayed "in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the Allied forces' efforts during World War II."

More than eight decades after the ship failed to reach the battlefields of Europe, the Montgomery and its dangerous cargo will remain where it came to rest, now entirely hidden from view, but far from forgotten.

title: Israel vows major West Bank operation after attack kills 2 troops
summary: Israel's Netanyahu says he ordered the military to cordon off a major city in the occupied West Bank after an attack by Palestinian gunmen that killed two Israeli soldiers.
story: Tel Aviv — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that he had ordered a major military operation in the occupied West Bank and told troops to cordon off a large city in the territory after a shooting attack by two Palestinian men that killed two soldiers.

The Israeli military said forces killed the Palestinian gunmen after they opened fire at a junction near the West Bank city of Hebron. The military later confirmed that two soldiers, Staff Sergeant Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem, were killed in the attack, while three others were lightly injured.
Netanyahu said he had ordered the evacuation of residents from the neighborhood in Hebron where the gunmen lived ahead of a house-to-house sweep for weapons.
"Our first step will be to demolish this site and completely transform it," Netanyahu said.
He added that he ordered the IDF to cordon off Hebron, a city with more than 200,000 inhabitants. Netanyahu said a broader military operation would follow.

"The IDF will enter the neighborhoods from which the terrorists emerged, evacuate the residents, go house-to-house, and dismantle the terror infrastructure. We are prepared for an extensive operation in Judea and Samaria," he said, using Israel's name for the West Bank.

Israel's military said a large amount of weapons and ammunition was discovered in the attackers' vehicle, alleging that they were planning a major attack on civilians. The shooters used an M16 rifle and a handgun in their attack, the IDF said.
The escalation in the West Bank comes just before Israel holds elections on Tuesday, in which Netanyahu has made national security a central issue of his campaign for another term.

Netanyahu said the Palestinian shooting attack was an attempt to influence Israel elections, and referenced a warning he made a few weeks ago about Israel's enemies preparing attacks to affect the vote.
Netanayhu called the gunmen involved in the shooting near Hebron "Hamas terrorists."
Hamas called the attack heroic and a legitimate response to "ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people, land, and holy sites," but the group stopped short of claiming responsibility.

Hamas, long designated a terrorist group by Israel and the U.S., called for any Palestinians in the West Bank with guns to use them to attack Israeli soldiers and civilians living in the occupied territory.

Following the shooting, the IDF said it had launched "offensive counterterrorism operations" in the Hebron area, and that soldiers were operating inside the residences of the shooters in Friday's attack and other suspects.
The IDF said it had arrested around 70 wanted Palestinians during operations in the West Bank over the past week.
Netanyahu's Likud party said the prime minister had convened his top security chiefs Friday, and that the party was canceling all campaign events for the rest of the day.

The attack follows a recent surge in Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians. It also comes after Brad Lander, a New York Democratic candidate for Congress, was briefly detained by Israeli forces this week while helping Palestinian farmers during the annual olive harvest.
