title: Personalized mRNA vaccine for melanoma cut risk of cancer’s return in late-stage trial
summary: Moderna and Merck’s personalized mRNA vaccine for melanoma reduced the risk of cancer recurrence and death by 42% compared with standard treatment in a trial.
story: A new personalized mRNA vaccine for melanoma is being hailed by some oncologists as a major breakthrough after it reduced the risk of cancer recurrence and death by 42% compared with standard treatment in a late-stage clinical trial.
Dr. Robert Vonderheide, director of Penn Medicine’s Abramson Cancer Center and president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, said the results are a “game changer.”
“It will be seen as the first step toward using cancer vaccines to their full potential,” said Vonderheide, who was not involved in the trial.

The experimental vaccine, called intismeran, was developed by drugmakers Moderna and Merck. Intismeran is personalized to each patient, using genomic data from the patient’s tumor. The new results will be presented Saturday at the annual meeting of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Madrid.
The trial included 1,137 Stage 3 melanoma patients. All of the participants had undergone surgery to remove their tumors and were being treated with Merck’s immunotherapy drug Keytruda.

In addition to Keytruda, 757 of the participants also got the personalized vaccine; the remaining 380 got a placebo. Two years later, 82% of the patients who received both the new vaccine and the immunotherapy hadn’t had a recurrence, compared with 70% in the immunotherapy plus placebo group.

In Stage 3 melanoma, the cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes or other sites on the skin, but it hasn’t spread to distant organs. Cancer recurrence is the “dreaded event” for these patients, Vonderheide said. If it does return, spread to distant organs is more likely.

Dr. Georgina Long, co-medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia who led the clinical trial, said that while scans might suggest that melanoma has been completely removed by surgery, invisible cancer cells may still be lurking.
“This treatment is about mopping up the cancer cells we can’t see,” Long said. “We know with [Keytruda] alone, that works really well, but not in everyone.”

Keytruda works by mobilizing immune cells called T cells to spot and destroy cancer. The vaccine also helps the immune system fight cancer. Each vaccine is created by taking the excised tumor, sequencing its genome and identifying a tell-tale fingerprint of abnormal proteins known as neoantigens, Long said. The vaccine trains the immune system to recognize and target these neoantigens, similar to how a standard vaccine is trained to recognize and target a virus or bacteria.

Intismeran uses messenger RNA technology, the same platform pioneered in the development of Covid vaccines that’s hailed for how quickly it can be rolled out. Each patient received their personalized vaccine in a little over nine weeks on average.
“They’re not on the shelf,” Vonderheide said. “They have to be made for that patient. Can that be done in a few weeks in order to have a timely treatment? Turns out, the answer to that is yes.”

Dr. Shirin Bajaj, incoming director of hHead and nNeck mMelanoma at Mount Sinai in New York, said that while Keytruda works by taking the brakes off the immune system and enabling it to recognize cancer cells, the new vaccine is likely enhancing its abilities by mobilizing additional immune cells called killer T cells.
“It essentially creates an army of killer T cells that are meant to recognize the tumor,” said Bajaj, who was not involved in the trial.
Side effects of the vaccine included pain around the injection site and a mild fever — similar to those seen with Covid vaccines.

For Dr. Gino In, an associate professor at the USC Keck School of Medicine Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center in Los Angeles, that is a major selling point. In some cases, Keytruda can result in serious organ inflammation, and previous attempts to combine the immunotherapies with other drugs have not only failed to improve cancer recurrence outcomes, but resulted in worse side effects.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“In prior trials, other drugs that were studied in combination with [this class of immunotherapies] led to significant, and eventually potentially permanent side effects, particularly side effects that triggered the immune system to attack our own body,” In, who wasn’t involved with the trial, wrote in an email.

Despite the positive results, investors reacted poorly when the findings were leaked on Thursday, causing Moderna’s stock price to fall. Bajaj said that this may be because while the trial’s results are a significant breakthrough for the field of cancer vaccines, the difference between taking Keytruda and the vaccine compared with Keytruda alone is still relatively modest.

“The reality is that on one hand, any difference you see is amazing because it’s one more option for a patient,” she said. “Is this likely helpful for a handful of patients? I would say yes, but it’s hard to say whether at this point we have data to suggest that this is actually the next blockbuster.”

The full data is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal, and Bajaj said that the patients in the trial still need to be followed for several more years to see whether the vaccine continues to offer additional benefits in terms of preventing the return and spread of melanoma as well as its effects on survival.

In addition, Bajaj said she had questions over the scalability of the treatment. She noted that of the 1,749 melanoma patients who were initially screened for participation in the trial, 17% did not have tumor samples that were big enough for a vaccine to be created.

“It’s amazing, but I think some of the logistics are going to need to be worked out,” she said. “But nothing that I saw from this study made me think that the logistics are infeasible. It’s just that it will be a hurdle to actually do this at a wide scale.”

However, Vonderheide described the results as a very welcome boost for the field of cancer vaccines. In recent months, the German company BioNTech announced clinical trial failures for experimental vaccines for colorectal and head and neck cancers.
He suggested that intismeran’s success may be because the Merck and Moderna trial focused on preventing melanoma recurrence rather than prolonging survival in later stage patients.

“The field of cancer vaccines has been filled with disappointments in treating patients with advanced disease,” Vonderheide said. “Some people look at those results and say, ‘cancer vaccines will never work.’ These results show that cancer vaccines are incredibly powerful when deployed in the right clinical setting. Vaccines work to prevent.”
Still, intismeran is being studied in a separate clinical trial in patients with advanced melanoma that has already spread to distant organs.
“This is just the proof of concept,” Long said. “We’re going into advanced melanoma, but we’re also doing work in many other cancers — bladder cancer, kidney cancer, lung cancer, using this concept.”
She said that researchers will also be actively working to understand more about why the vaccine worked to see if that can lead to further clues.

Vonderheide described the future possibilities for preventing cancer recurrence as being myriad. “One day, we might be able to think of how to use a cancer vaccine to prevent cancer in the first place,” he said. “That’s a very ambitious, far-off goal. But these results bring that goal even closer to reality than we might think.”

title: Hero who stopped Bend school shooter haunted by encounter: ‘I didn’t save everybody’
summary: Kaylub Giamanco speaks for the first time about the day he brought down a school shooter in Bend, Oregon.
story: A string of innocuous choices made by an Oregon father brought him to the elementary school where he killed a mass shooter in an intervention the dad believed would be his last act on earth.
Police have credited the quick thinking and decisive action of Bend carpenter Kaylub Giamanco for confronting 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and stopping the teen shooter’s carnage.

The gunman had already killed a teacher and three young children at Silver Rail Elementary School on Oct. 15 and could have continued his attack had Giamanco, 36, not randomly ended up at the crime scene.
In an emotional and harrowing interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting published on Friday, Giamanco recalled that fateful day.

“I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small. I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family,” he told OPB. “I feel like if I’m going to have a voice, then I’ll be damned if I’m not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place.”
Giamanco’s presence in the neighborhood near Silver Rail came after a series of seemingly benign decisions the carpenter made that Thursday about lunch.
Giamanco packed a mid-day snack but changed his mind about eating it, instead opting to drive home to have leftover tacos with his wife, he said.
And on his way home, Giamanco had briefly considered going to a masonry shop to buy some bolts he needed, but again opted to go home for the tacos.

Those choices led him to Brentwood Avenue near his children’s school just before 1 p.m., where he spotted a “man in black” with a long gun opening fire on a motorist and a woman mowing the school lawn, he recalled.
Giamanco, who kept a .40 caliber handgun in his truck console, saw the killer toss his weapon over the school fence before climbing it himself.
The father understood what was happening and “that’s when panic filled into my brain, and that’s when I opened my center console.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Giamanco, who has two girls, 5 and 10, attending Silver Rail,  called 911 but couldn’t answer all of the dispatcher’s questions.
“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” said Giamanco.
As Giamanco got closer to the school building, he kept a low profile and from his knees could hear the bloodshed.

“That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives and then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster and I told myself, ‘This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do,’” he said.
Giamanco crawled in through a shot out window, reached the special education classroom and re-racked his firearm in preparation for a deadly confrontation.
He came upon the gunman and a teacher fighting for the killer’s gun.
“I knew that he did not know that I was there,” Giamanco said. “And I fired.”
The teacher fled, possibly believing Giamanco was a second attacker, he said. But the shooter was still alive and reaching for his gun.
“He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.”
Police arrived shortly after and Giamanco pleaded with them to let him call his loved ones.
“I called my wife to tell her that I’m not coming home for tacos,” he said.
Then he called his mother.
“She was just like, ‘Okay, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You’re a hero. You saved lives.’ And I was just like, “I didn’t save everybody. I didn’t get them all.’”

Law enforcement officials have universally praised Giamanco for acting fast. Within hours of the shooting, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said of Giamanco and the teacher who fought with the killer: “I don’t think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage.”
Giamanco said he’s been struggling to sleep since the mass shooting and can’t get that terrible day out of his head.
“I relive, I see faces, I hear voices, I hear screams,” he said.
The carpenter has not yet met the parents of the three children killed. Giamanco said he wants to tell them he’s sorry for not doing more.
“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco said, his voice choking with emotion. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”

title: Trump doubles down on defending Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton
summary: President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his support of a widely condemned attack ad against Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton
story: President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his support of a widely condemned attack ad against Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, saying that he won’t change his mind about the $4 million ad campaign by her Republican opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, that features her estranged mother calling her a “liar.”

Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump was asked if he has changed his mind about defending the minutelong ad, now that he knows the backstory about Acton’s late stepfather, whom Acton has said sexually abused her as a child.
“No, it’s a mother speaking badly against Amy Acton,” Trump said. “If it were my mother speaking badly about me, you’d be making it the No. 1 story on the news.”
Trump also criticized an NBC News reporter who pressed him further about the situation, calling her “a fresh person” and “horrible little reporter.”
Asked by NBC News about Republicans who have denounced the ad, Trump said “They don’t know the facts.”
“A mother is saying, ‘Don’t put my daughter there, because she’s a terrible person and she’s a liar.’ Why shouldn’t somebody use that?” he added.

The president first voiced support for the ad in a post on Truth Social Thursday, suggesting that Republicans were being treated unfairly. “If my mother, the legendary Mary MacLeod Trump, said anything bad about me, the Fake News would play it up,” Trump wrote. “The Dumocrats would be totally supportive, and it would go down as the Ad of the Decade — Maybe the Century!”
He then addressed the controversy in remarks at a campaign rally in Sioux City, Iowa at night, claiming that Ramaswamy asked him what to do amid the media firestorm.
“I said, ‘You got to ride with it,’” Trump recounted.

Ramaswamy defended the ad at a campaign bus tour stop in Strongsville, Ohio, Friday morning. He accused the “flawed and failed media” of “lying about an ad that is about lying.” His campaign told NBC News on Thursday that it planned a $4 million push to air the ad.

“It had nothing to do with childhood abuse, which I will be the No. 1 governor to prosecute when I am the governor of this state, because it is wrong and we together will fight against that across Ohio. That is the truth — that they’re changing the subject because they don’t want to answer for their own failures,” Ramaswamy told a crowd of supporters.

Documents obtained by NBC News from the Mahoning County Clerk of Courts show Acton’s stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and indicted by a grand jury in 1978 in Ohio for rape involving a child under 13 years old between 1976 and 1978. While the victim’s name is redacted in the records, Acton’s biological father, Gerald Stearns, signed one of the documents.
At the White House, a reporter noted that Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, stood by the stepfather during the trial. “Look, you don’t know that,” Trump said. “You don’t know anything.”
Acton has said she has not seen or spoken to her mother in nearly 50 years. Arthur has not responded to requests for comment.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“Her mother went on television and said that the daughter who’s running for governor of Ohio is a liar and a bad person, and that’s all I know,” Trump said.

Trump continued, “The press is embarrassing themselves. You’re trying to take a horrible situation for a Democrat and make it look better. The mother said really bad things about a person that wants to be the Democrat governor of Ohio. The mother said terrible things. Anybody seeing that would say, ‘No way, I’m voting for her.’”

Trump said that Acton’s mother looks “very lucid” and “very smart” in the ad. After the spot surfaced Monday, Acton’s campaign described it as an “attempt to platform” an “estranged and abusive mother.”

“If my mother said bad things about me, you think the Democrats would put it up? I think so. But my mother thought I was wonderful. Thank you, Mom,” Trump said. “This has nothing to do with the stepfather or anything else.”

While Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended the ad, a number of Republicans have condemned it. Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, rebuked it on Thursday, telling reporters, “The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling.” He called on Ramaswamy to take it down, but said he still supports the entire Republican ticket in Ohio, including Ramaswamy.

Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who faces a competitive re-election race, also criticized it, saying he wouldn’t have run the ad. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has previously spoken about being a sexual assault victim, called it “the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.” And Iowa Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, who also faces a tight general election race, condemned the ad.

““It’s terrible. I think about it as a mom and you think about your kids surviving childhood sexual abuse and having to relive that trauma on TV again. I think it’s absolutely terrible, and I think they should take the ad down,” she said in an interview with ABC News on Thursday.

During a campaign stop in Cincinnati on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance responded to the backlash from within his party, telling them to “stop whining” about the ad and to focus on winning midterm elections.

“Politics is a tough business,” Vance said. “And my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days.”

title: How Starlink slowdown hit Ukraine’s front line soldiers pushing Russia back
summary: The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine.
story: The drone unit he leads has been helping push back Russian troops on the front lines in southeastern Ukraine. Then, late last Tuesday, a drone launched toward Russian troops suddenly lost connection.

“As it was picking up speed, contact with the drone was lost in an instant,” according to the commander, 47, who is serving on the border between the eastern Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia regions, and only wanted to be identified by his call sign Flint due to the sensitivity of his service.
The drone fell to the ground, aborting the mission, Flint said in a series of messages on WhatsApp. He fears the technology inside “may have fallen into enemy hands.”
“Only after analyzing the flight, it became clear that the issue was specifically related to the Starlink speed limit,” he added.

Ukraine said last week that limits were imposed without warning on its use of Starshield, the military variant of the Starlink internet service run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, affecting battlefield missions reliant on it.

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Musk had restored the service in Ukraine, but Kyiv said Friday that it was not seeing any lifting of restrictions. Trump did not say why the limits were in place, though Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS.”  Ukraine had also warned of gaps in intelligence sharing from the U.S., something the White House has denied.

title: DOJ sues to block Alaska Senate certification if GOP’s Dan Sullivan loses
summary: The Justice Department is suing Alaska election officials to prevent them from certifying Senate race results if GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan loses next month.
story: The Justice Department has filed suit against Alaska election officials, seeking to block the results of November’s U.S. Senate election from being certified unless incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan wins — a controversial move President Donald Trump claimed credit for.
In papers filed in federal court, attorneys for the DOJ argued the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot could mislead supporters of the sitting senator, Daniel S. Sullivan.
“For example, some supporters of Senator Sullivan likely will inadvertently vote for Daniel J. Sullivan,” the filing says.
“To guard against this danger, it is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” the suit says.

The Trump administration is seeking a court order blocking the results from being certified “if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sullivan and Alaska’s rank-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”
Trump told reporters Friday that he directed the suit to be filed.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump said, calling Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy “a disgrace.”
The filing by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said the action was brought “to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.”

The Trump administration filed the lawsuit Thursday, the same day Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters that “it is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state confirmation process or certification process.”
“I’m not trying to not have an election certified. Of course not,” Blanche said, although there could be some “doomsday” scenario in which DOJ would seek to get involved.
It’s unclear why the department decided to seek action now, with Election Day less than two weeks away.
U.S. elections are run by state and local officials, who are charged with certifying results.
The Justice Department’s role in U.S. elections is limited by law, which chiefly allows the department to safeguard civil rights and prosecute people who violate election law.

While private citizens and candidates can sue to challenge ballots or election results, Justin Levitt, an NBC News contributor who was a Justice Department official during the Obama administration, said there’s no law that says DOJ can challenge ballots or delay certification.

A DOJ spokesperson told NBC News in a statement that Sullivan’s “candidacy was intended to mislead voters and compromise the fairness of the ballot. Therefore, the Justice Department, consistent with the National Voter Registration Act enacted by Congress, is taking the necessary steps to ensure that this frivolous candidacy does not undermine the integrity of Alaska’s election or the will of its voters.”
A DOJ official called the situation “unique.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
David Becker,  executive director for the non-profit Center for Election Innovation & Research, called the legal action “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government” in a statement.

“This is purely a matter of state law, and the administration has absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election,” he said, and the “DOJ attempting to intervene at this late stage is entirely against department policy.”

Sullivan Jr.’s candidacy has already been challenged in Alaska, where in August he finished in third place with 2.5% of the vote in the all-party primary. Democrat Mary Peltola received 49.5% and Sen. Sullivan received 41.4%.

Sullivan Jr. was initially booted from the ballot in June after election officials found his candidacy was not in “good faith,” citing his choice to run using the name Dan instead of Daniel and being “affiliated with the Republican Party” when he had previously “never — according to the Division’s records — been affiliated with the Republican Party in Alaska.”
The Alaska courts, however, ruled he could stay on the ballot.

The November ballot does differentiate the two Sullivans. “Dan S. Sullivan” is listed with a “registered Republican” and “incumbent” next to his name, while the other is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.” with no party affiliation next to his name.
Sullivan Jr. did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Sullivan’s campaign and his Republican allies have charged Sullivan Jr. is a Democratic dupe, being used to draw votes away from the incumbent. Trump has repeatedly criticized Sullivan Jr. as a “cheat.”

“It’s cheating. It’s a spoiler candidate to go on the ballot with the exact same name as your great Senator Dan Sullivan. This guy’s name is Dan Sullivan. He knew nothing about politics. He was just put there by the Democrats to confuse the voter, and it’s very unfair. But that’s what they do. They cheat. They lie. They steal,” Trump said in a video post on social media earlier this month.

NBC News reported back in July that federal and state investigators were looking at whether Sullivan Jr. could be part of a conspiracy to confuse voters, citing two people with knowledge of the matter. The status of that investigation is unclear.
A spokesperson for Peltola said earlier this year that her “campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
Sullivan Jr., a former teacher, told The Associated Press back in June that his candidacy is no sham and that he’s not in cahoots with anybody.

“I have every right to run for whatever office I’m qualified for, and I’m qualified for this office,” he said then. “I think I’m doing what most Americans would think would be a patriotic thing to do when you’re unsatisfied with the status quo. You stand up and say, ‘I’m going to fight for things I believe that are going to make my community better.’”

title: Mississippi police officer who fatally shot 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned
summary: The Mississippi police officer who fired the shot that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned, a city official told NBC News on Friday.
story: The Mississippi police officer who fired the shot that killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley has resigned, a city official told NBC News on Friday.

Hunter Foster, who worked for the Senatobia Police Department, turned in his badge and gun just a few days after state Attorney General Lynn Fitch’s office issued a brief statement saying the fatal shooting was a “justified” use of force.
Jada Mayer, who is Senatobia’s human resources clerk, did not say why Foster was leaving the Senatobia Police Department.
“The mayor’s office confirmed the resignation,” Mayer said.
Foster’s lawyer, Martin Zummach, said in an email to NBC News that Foster “resigned for the good of the city and the police department and to permit the process of healing.”

“He is still shocked and sickened that a baby died and emphatically denies knowing a child was in the car or in the front seat and had no idea that those fleeing were suspected of shoplifting,” the lawyer said.

While the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has stated that police had been responding to the Walmart to investigate a shoplifting,  Zummach wrote Foster was part of a team “investigating an unrelated case involving an adult who had attempted to sexually assault a minor on the store’s property.”
“All that Foster and the other law enforcement present were told during that investigation process is that ‘they are running,’” Zummach wrote.
The fatal shooting of Kohen on June 14 caused an uproar in this small town some 40 miles south of Memphis, Tennessee, where Black residents have long complained about police harassment.

The shooting happened after the officers responding to a report of a shoplifting at a local Walmart arrived and saw “two subjects and a juvenile child fleeing from the store into a vehicle,” according to the MBI.
Kohen’s mother, whom her lawyer identified as Vellesiya Wiley, was a passenger. Her friend was driving. Both women are Black, as was Kohen.

“Officers attempted to stop the vehicle, but the driver drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one,” the MBI said in a June 14 report. “An officer then discharged their weapon and the vehicle fled the scene. The subjects arrived at a local hospital where one juvenile child in the vehicle was pronounced deceased, and another subject had critical injuries.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Kohen’s mother has disputed that account.

Her lawyer, Ben Crump, posted a video on social media in June where Wiley said they had gone to Walmart for diapers. She said that her friend was briefly stopped while they were leaving the store and that “I kept walking because it had nothing to do with me.”
“By the time me and my baby got in the car, she came,” Wiley said of her friend.
They encountered police as they began to back out, Wiley said.
“I raised my baby up trying to show them that he was in the car,” she said.
In that moment, Wiley said her friend inadvertently hit another car while Wiley’s door was open.
On Thursday, the Mississippi Department of Public Safety released video showing the same shooting from multiple law enforcement officers’ body-worn cameras.

They show two women, one holding a baby, running across the parking lot and entering a vehicle. Five officers approach the parked car with guns drawn. The car reverses away and crashes into a parked vehicle nearby as officers yell for it to stop.

The vehicle then accelerates forward as an officer steps toward it with his gun drawn. The wheels turn away from him, and he appears to put his hands on the hood as he jumps out of the way. He fires his gun, shattering the window of the front passenger side. The car continues to drive away before the video cuts out.

title: Ohio father charged with killing sheriff deputy found guilty
summary: An Ohio father accused of mowing down a deputy with his car hours after he viewed body camera video of a Cincinnati police officer fatally shooting his son was found guilty Friday of charges including murder.
story: An Ohio father accused of mowing down a deputy with his car hours after he viewed body camera video of a Cincinnati police officer fatally shooting his son was found guilty Friday of charges including murder.
The jury began deliberating Wednesday morning following days of testimony in Rodney L. Hinton’s murder trial, NBC affiliate WLWT of Cincinnati reported.
Hinton is scheduled to be sentenced on November 16.

Just hours before the May 2025 crash that killed Hamilton County Special Deputy Larry Henderson, Hinton had been called to the police station to watch body camera video of his 18-year-old son  fatally shot by a Cincinnati officer.

Police had responded to a report of a stolen vehicle at an apartment complex. Authorities said Hinton’s son, Ryan Hinton, was among a group of people in the allegedly stolen car, and some of them ran when officers approached.
Two officers pursued Ryan Hinton, who police said was armed, and another person.

In video released by police, an officer exits his vehicle and points his gun at Ryan Hinton, who appears to be running away. The officer fired at least four shots, police said at a news conference last year. In another video, an officer yells, “He’s got a gun!” Authorities said the gun was recovered from the scene.

In closing arguments, defense attorney Clyde Bennett II said Hinton had struggled with mental health in the past and that his family was worried about him after he watched the video. Bennett asked the jury to find Hinton not guilty by reason of insanity.
Prosecutors said Henderson saw the car coming at the last second and stepped out of the way, but Hinton “tracked him.”

“He turned his wheel the same direction that Larry moved, and the car struck Larry, throwing him, tossing him into the air, twisting him until he landed,” Assistant Prosecutor Kate Burroughs said in closing arguments.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Burroughs said Hinton’s vehicle went from 0 to over 43 mph in seconds and the accelerator was pressed 93.3%.
“Everything that happened that day was in the driver’s hands,” she said.

During the trial, the defense’s expert witness testified that Hinton did not know right from wrong at the time of the crash, according to WLWT. The state’s rebuttal witness testified that Hinton was grieving and angry but knew his actions were wrong.
Henderson’s wife also took the stand and became emotional as she discussed their last moments together before he left for work, the news station reported.
“He looked at me, and he said, ‘I love you,’ and I remember adding, I said back, ‘I love you too,’” Lori Henderson said, crying.
Henderson had retired from the sheriff’s office about five months before the crash and was working as a special deputy directing traffic near the University of Cincinnati during graduation.

title: DOJ charges two former top FBI officials who were frequent targets of Trump allies
summary: Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump over their intelligence work during the 2020 presidential election have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress.
story: WASHINGTON — Two former FBI officials who have come under withering criticism from allies of President Donald Trump have been charged with allegedly lying to Congress over the investigation into former President Joe Biden’s son Hunter Biden.

A court docket shows that Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another FBI official, were facing one count of the rarely-charged criminal offense which can be difficult to prosecute.
Hunter Biden was investigated, charged and eventually convicted of  gun and tax crimes, before his father pardoned him shortly leaving office.

U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a social media post that Floris and Benavides had surrendered Friday morning. She alleged that the duo lied about their roles in the Foreign Influence Task Force and “about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.”

Attorneys for Floris said in a statement that Floris was “a patriot” who “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years” and was charged so the administration could “push a false narrative for a shot at political points.”

Attorneys Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle R. Freeny said in a statement that the “DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”

One of the attorneys for Benavides, Ronald S. Safer, called the charges a disgrace and said Friday that his client “worked tirelessly to protect the public from terrorists and agents of foreign governments” for 20 years and “protected our democracy against those who would destroy it.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“In return, today, the government that he loves brought baseless criminal charges against him in a transparently political complaint,” Safer said. “This is another sad day for the Department of Justice. But now we are in court, and the truth will come out: Brad Benavides is a true patriot who devoted his career to protecting this country and its people.”

The case was brought through a criminal complaint. Neither defendant has yet been indicted by a federal grand jury in D.C., where grand jurors have been skeptical of cases brought during Trump’s second term. Earlier this year, federal grand jurors rejected an attempt to indict six sitting Democratic members of Congress over a video Trump criticized.

Flores was the FBI’s security lead for the 2020 presidential election, which Trump has falsely claimed was stolen. A mob of Trump supporters violently broke into the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021, in a failed effort to stop the certification of Democrat Joe Biden as president. They beat and bloodied law enforcement, shattered windows and broke through barriers.

She joined the FBI as an intelligence analyst in 2005, working on the director’s daily briefing staff and helped produce intelligence documents. She was promoted in 2017 to the department’s counterterrorism division.
Benavides is a former colleague of Floris who focused on election security, foreign influence and Chinese intelligence threats.
Floris has also been under criticism from Republicans over emails in which she discussed intelligence work that were obtained by Congress and declassified in July by Trump.
Republicans have alleged that FBI officials buried what they describe as a credible report on China’s efforts to influence the election in an effort to protect then-FBI Director Christopher Wray.
Intelligence officials and her legal team have said the pullback was a standard administrative move for a report that may have been unverified or had flawed intelligence.

title: Etsy to restrict AI-generated content in effort to combat seller slop
summary: Etsy announced new restrictions on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud.
story: Etsy announced new restrictions Thursday on AI-generated content on its platform, saying it threatens the integrity of its sellers’ work and leaves buyers exposed to fraud.
Among the new stipulations:

Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.Bot-generated listings are banned.
Patterns, recipes, or any other item that involves a buyer “putting in effort to achieve a finished product” cannot be created using AI.
Sellers must include at least one unaltered photo of the actual item against a real background.
Bot-generated listings are banned.
AI-generated art can still be sold on the platform as long as merchants “Play a clear role in what they create and are transparent about the process,” Etsy said in a note to sellers.
“Our marketplace only works when buyers and sellers trust each other,” Etsy Vice President of Customer Operations James Ossman wrote in a blog post.

“Sellers need clear guidance and confidence that their creativity and craftsmanship will be represented fairly; buyers need to understand what they’re buying and the human involvement behind it. We know we have work to do to uphold this standard on Etsy.”
Etsy hosts more than 5 million entrepreneurs, most of whom are women who run one-person businesses out of their homes, according to an annual company report.
For Subscribers

That distinguishes it from other major e-commerce platforms like Amazon and eBay, though it commands a fraction of those platforms’ revenues. As of 2024, Etsy hosted $10.9 billion-worth of goods’ sales, compared with about $75 billion for eBay and more than $700 billion for Amazon.
Some buyers responded positively to Etsy’s announcement.

“I can’t explain how infuriating it has been to purchase a crochet pattern, only to open the PDF and realize it’s fully AI-generated, doesn’t make sense, and definitely doesn’t match what the finished product should be,” creator Kara Lynne said on X.
The dawn of advanced AI has led to an explosion in AI-generated sales content — and a growing backlash from consumers against what they see as AI slop.
For Subscribers
A recent social media trend among cafes and restaurants saw owners pledging not to use AI after egregious examples of AI-generated food images in the wild were shared on social media.
Major platforms are responding to the growing discontent. Many, including Facebook and Instagram, now work to append labels to images or videos created via AI.
Others, like LinkedIn, have added buttons allowing users to report AI-generated content.
Snap has banned wholly AI-generated content from its recommendation algorithm, while Spotify recently announced it had removed 50 million AI-generated tracks from its platform.
Ossman said Etsy would add a function similar to LinkedIn’s that makes it easier for users to report listings that include misleading AI imagery.
He also said Etsy would be using technology to identify misleading imagery and fraudulent listings, with the goal of expanding removals of illicit listings in the coming months.
“We’re actively working to address the questions AI raises for our marketplace,” Ossman said in the post.
“This work is hard, and we don’t have every answer today. But I believe this is an important moment for Etsy, and that these initial steps are putting us on the right path.”

title: Marshall Faulk, Hall of Fame running back, reveals he has Parkinson’s disease
summary: Hall of Fame running back and Southern University football coach Marshall Faulk revealed that he’s been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and hopes early detection will give him chances “at living a better quality of life.”
story: Hall of Fame running back and Southern University football coach Marshall Faulk revealed that he’s been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease and hopes early detection will give him chances “at living a better quality of life.”
The 53-year-old made the announcement on “The Caring Neurologist” podcast on Wednesday, telling host Dr. Sandeep Thakkar that he hopes others will look out for early symptoms in themselves.

“What you want to do with that information is pass it on to the next generation to make sure that they have it better. that they know more,” Faulk said. “And you’re doing the leave this world a better place than it was, you know, when I got here.”
The progressive nervous system disorder affects more than a million Americans.
Faulk said he has been living with the condition for about 18 months and has experienced some hand rigidity and tremors.

“I think I caught it early and I’m in a good place,” the football icon said. ”I didn’t look at it like I got a diagnosis, it was something bad that I was, you know, life was going to end. Now, if you don’t take care of it, there’s an opportunity for that to be, but you have to take care of it.”
The coach is optimistic that medications can, at least in the immediate future, stave off the most serious symptoms of Parkinson’s.

“The earlier you catch it, the better chance you have at living a better quality of life with medication compared to if you catch it later, then you, the things that you start to have, the things that you go through, it makes life a little bit more difficult,” he said.
Faulk said he took inspiration from meeting Muhammad Ali in the boxer’s later years as the champ fought Parkinson’s.

“I sat next to him and he leaned over to me and he whispered, ‘You a bad boy,’” Faulk fondly recalled of having dinner with Ali. “And then he made a couple other comments. I was like, ‘He’s all there.’”
Faulk played 12 years in the NFL, seven for the then-St. Louis Rams and five for the Indianapolis Colts. He rushed for 12,279 yards, 13th most in league history.
But it Faulk’s ability to catch the football which made him one of the game’s most dangerous weapons. His 19,514 total yards from scrimmage ranks 5th all-time.
Faulk and his “Greatest Show on Turf” Rams won the 2000 Super Bowl, in a game best known for Mike Jones’ game-saving tackle of Kevin Dyson at the Rams’ 1-yard line as time expired.
Faulk caught 5 passes for 90 yards in that game played at the Georgia Dome.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The No. 2 overall pick in 1994 out of San Diego State  was inducted into Canton in 2011.
He is in his first season as head coach at Southern and the Jaguars are 3-4.  Southern plays Saturday against Texas Southern at Reliant Stadium in Houston.
Representatives for Southern could did immediately respond to an NBC News request for comment on Friday.
Faulk said he’s not yet experienced any cognitive issues. Parkinson’s can bring sleep, memory, problem solving and other brain-related challenges.
“My brain’s fine,” the coach said. “I feel clear of thought and I guess that’s a good thing.”
Faulk said he’s aware of difficulties that could be in his future and is already taking steps to more clearly organize his thoughts.
“Life has been, I want to say, normal,” the Hall of Fame running back said. “I take better notes, I’m more concise when I’m doing interviews.”

title: We swapped streaming for the $99 Lola CD player — here’s our honest review
summary: We tested the Lola CD Player for two weeks to see how it measures up to streaming services. Here’s who it’s best for and whether it’s worth the price.
story: Listening to music is easier than ever — you have hundreds of thousands of songs at your fingertips, plus, algorithms, custom playlists, pre-saves and more make the process feel automated. However, that doesn’t mean we’re ready to give up on physical media. A 2025 Consumer Reports study found that almost half of Americans (45%) still listen to CDs, with one in five still listening to vinyl records.

The Lola CD player is designed to help bring that nostalgic feel back to your music, and myself, along with three other NBC Selected editors, tested it for two weeks. We collectively agree that it’s a fun way to switch up our listening habits (and a very cute accessory to carry around), however, it may not be best for people most concerned with convenience. Keep reading to hear our thoughts and our final verdict on the CD player’s highs and lows.
Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter.
What to know about the Lola Portable CD Player
Lola Portable CD Player
Anti-skip featureLong battery lifeHeadphones included
Anti-skip feature

No BluetoothOnly 3.5mm jack
No Bluetooth

The Lola CD player is a classic portable player with a few modern updates, including anti-skip protection and a micro SD card slot. It charges via an included USB-C cable, so you can share a charger with your phone if needed. While the player doesn’t have Bluetooth capabilities, it has a 3.5mm headphone jack, and can be paired with a Bluetooth device with a third-party adapter, according to the brand. It also comes with a pair of polka dot, wired headphones, and gets up to 48 hours of playback on a single charge.
How we tested it

Four NBC Selected editors, myself included, tested courtesy samples for around two weeks, using it as a substitute for streaming music. We listened on commutes, on walks and throughout the day to see how the listening experience measured up. Since a few of us belong to different generations, we all have a range of experiences with physical media, helping to shape each of our unique perspectives on using the CD player.

While I’ve owned boomboxes and CD players in the past, two of our editors grew up listening to CDs, which made this testing process especially interesting for them. “I’m in my late 30s, and grew up recording songs off the radio onto cassette tapes and listening to them on my Walkman,” says NBC Selected senior editor Nikki Brown. “I eventually graduated to CDs, most of which I still have today — and of course I took my CD player everywhere,” she says.

NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans had a similar experience — “I’m a Xennial, so I had a Discman in high school and remember burning mixtapes in college,” she says. “I praised the day the iPod dropped and changed the way we listened to music”.

NBC Selected editorial operations associate (and Gen-Z-er) Jem Alabi, on the other hand, specifically likes buying physical versions of her favorite K-pop albums, but hasn’t had anything to play them on until now. “I have quite a few CD’s that have been collecting dust,” she says. “The CD’s tend to have bonus tracks that you can’t always find on streaming so I was happy to get to hear my favorite groups in this intimate way.”
Along with seeing how well the CD player works in comparison to streaming, we also evaluated features like the battery life and the player’s anti-skip protection.
What we liked

In our experience, the Lola CD player is worth it for anyone looking to invest more in physical media, or who may be searching for a more intimate and intentional music listening experience than streaming can offer. We also like the anti-skip protection and battery life. While those features work well, we felt as though our experiences with the headphones were mixed, and that the CD player, while cute, isn’t very convenient to carry around.

The Lola CD player definitely feels like a throwback to a simpler time — pre-streaming and algorithms, when your listening experience felt a lot more personal and manual. I especially felt this during the time when I’d choose my CDs for the day — I usually chose one to start with inside the player, and then one more to bring along for variety. Choosing the CD every morning felt like I was curating my mood for the day, which added an intentionality to my music listening that isn’t always there with streaming.

“Using this CD player felt like stepping into a time machine,” says Brown. “I pulled out my CD case and immediately was transported to all that was happening in my life when I made or bought each one — the people I was spending time with, the city I lived in, the party I pregamed for, the person I was dating.” She also turned it into a communal experience: “I started sending pictures of CDs to my group chat and we went down rabbit holes seeing what certain singers and musicians were up to since we last listened to them.” she says. Evans felt similarly, saying that using the CD player shifted her daily listening habits from single songs to full albums. “I also rediscovered songs that I loved and hadn’t heard in forever because I rarely play full albums all the way out (versus spot-playing songs from different albums),” she says.

Alabi, who grew up listening to Afrobeat CDs with her family, also felt that the CD player helped her reconnect with those memories: “My family has a vast Afrobeat CD collection with songs that marked my childhood but can’t be found on streaming, so it was cool to have a way to preserve and revive those memories,” she says. That’s also something I loved about the CD player — it let me finally put so many of my old CDs to use while on-the-go, instead of letting them collect dust on my shelves (and made me look forward to picking up some new ones, too).

Prior to testing, one of Evans’ biggest concerns was whether or not the player would skip, or damage her CDs. Thankfully, the device’s anti-skip protection did its job well, which she calls “a huge plus”. She was also reminded that since the music didn’t rely on a Wi-Fi connection, there were no service outages. “This does not go down in ‘dead zones’ the way streaming does and that was a nice change,” she says. I also didn’t experience any skipping, which I fully expected, since it was such a common part of my experience with CD players when I was younger.
“I experienced skipping but only because I was listening to my mixed CDs that I would literally just throw into bags and commute with, without protection (ah, to be young!),” says Brown.

I used the CD player for a few hours daily, and only had to  charge it every few days. As someone who charges their phone not only overnight, but constantly throughout the day, it was nice to have a device that I didn’t have to think about plugging in. I also like that I didn’t feel the need to bring along the charger, like I do with my phone, since I knew the battery wouldn’t run out on me. Brown, who used the player every few days, had a similar experience and says hers still wasn’t close to needing another charge at the time of giving feedback.
Potential drawbacks to keep in mind

Our experiences with the headphones were varied. Brown, who doesn’t care too deeply about sound quality, says she thought the listening experience was good, and Evans felt similarly. “It was as good as any other device I use today,” says Evans. I, on the other hand, wasn’t a big fan of the sound quality, and felt the headphones had a far-away  sound, as if you were listening through a wall. Alabi felt similarly, saying that she thought “the headphones were cute but they felt and sounded kind of cheap, like the ones you get on the airplane.”  “I recommend using or buying another pair to enhance the listening experience,” she says.

We also all felt that in our experience, the volume, although not overpoweringly loud, was loud enough to be heard outside of the headphones. “People can clearly hear what you’re listening to and it’s loud since the corded earbuds don’t have ANC,” says Evans.

While the Lola CD player itself isn’t bulky, we didn’t exactly find it to be compact or slim either. If you’re carrying a larger or medium-sized bag, it shouldn’t pose any issues — “it’s kind of bulky but it did slide right into my bag with my laptop and planner,” says Evans. However, if you’re looking to carry along a mini bag (as I often do when I’m not at the office), you’ll either have to hold it in your hands, or leave the CD player behind.

The other size/portability consideration comes with the CDs. Again, you either have to choose to commit to one, or commit to carrying multiple around with you. Although the player’s CD card insert is designed to bypass that problem, you still have to load the memory cards with songs, which adds another manual step that streaming doesn’t require.
Is the Lola portable CD player worth it?

The Lola portable CD player is worth it if you’re looking to add a vintage twist to your music listening experience. It may not be ideal if you’re used to the convenience of streaming, but at its current price of $99, it’s best for those who either haven’t owned one before and would like to try, or who are trying to recapture the nostalgia of a bygone era.

“This is definitely more for someone who never knew what it was to lug around a book of CDs just to get through an hour-long commute,” says Evans. On the other hand, she also says that “one of the biggest pluses to this is rediscovering songs on full albums that I haven’t heard in so long and kind of forgot about (but love).” Brown agrees that the CD player has a universal appeal. “CD players are for everyone,” she says. “There’s something positive to be taken from the experience of using one, regardless of your age or background.”
Alternatives to consider

When it comes to retro tech, Urban Outfitters is one of my favorite destinations for browsing — the retailer has a wide range of options that are designed to be nostalgic, but with a modern twist. If you’re looking to recreate the CD experience at home, consider bookshelf players and boomboxes like the affordable Jenson CD590 boombox, or the more versatile Emerson EDL-2901 Multi-Media Boombox. You can also double down on the nostalgia and go for a record player, like the Crosley Eclipse Entertainment Center. If portability is what you’re after, MoMA Design Store’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has a cool transparent design, or you can get an MP3 player like the Globluum MP3 Player from Amazon.
Why trust NBC Selected?

I’m an associate SEO reporter for NBC Selected, covering skin care, lifestyle and more, along with being a longtime music fan and collector of records, CDs, magazines and more. I’ve written about why I love my old Sony bookshelf CD player, along with my Audio-Technica record player, and for this piece, myself and three other NBC Selected staffers tried out the Lola portable CD player, to see how the vintage device would hold up against our modern music habits.

title: This is the right way to use a neti pot, plus the best ones to buy
summary: Ear, nose and throat doctors explain whether neti pots are safe, how to use and clean one, and who should avoid them. Plus, shop highly-rated neti pots for cold season.
story: With cold and flu season here, you may be looking for ways to ease a stuffy nose without reaching for medication. Neti pots, the small teapot-shaped devices that rinse your nasal passages with a saline solution, are a popular option. They can help flush out mucus and irritants, but if you’ve never used one, pouring water into one nostril and out the other can feel odd or even a little intimidating.

To find out whether neti pots are safe for everyone and how to use one correctly, I asked two ear, nose and throat (ENT) doctors to walk me through it. Below, they explain what to know before you start and the steps to follow for a comfortable rinse. I also rounded up highly-rated neti pots to shop if you want to add one to your cold-season routine.
Are neti pots safe to use?
“A neti pot is a container [typically] shaped like a small teapot, used to flush out the nose and sinuses,” says Dr. Ryan Salvador, an ENT surgeon at Sinus and Snoring Specialists in Austin.

If you’re nervous about trying one, the experts say there’s no need to be. “Neti pots are safe and effective when used correctly,” says Dr. Madeleine Herman, an ENT physician and president of the Sinus Center and ENT Specialists of Houston. “They help rinse away thick mucus, allergens and other debris from the nose and can provide relief from congestion associated with colds, allergies and sinus problems.”

That said, there’s one rule you should never skip. “The quality of your water is the biggest safety concern,” says Herman. “Never use straight tap water in a neti pot. Use distilled or sterile water, or tap water that has been boiled and then cooled. This is important because organisms that may be harmless when swallowed can cause serious infections if they enter the nose.”
The best neti pots in 2026

Before you can use a neti pot, you need one. To put together a list of the best ones, I relied on guidance from experts on what to look for when shopping. Based on what they said, I sourced highly-rated options that have at least a four-star average rating from thousands of reviews. Just note: Neti pots should never be used with water straight from the tap, and you’ll need some sort of saline solution — almost all of the picks below come with saline packets.

These packets make nasal irrigation simple: just mix one packet with 8 ounces of distilled or boiled water. Each box holds 100 premixed packets of sodium chloride and sodium bicarbonate that help you create a saline solution to use in your neti pot. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans buys these for her neti pot after her doctor recommended them. “Depending on how often you rinse, this pack can last a really long time,” she says. “I feel like I haven’t had tore-up in forever.”
How to use a neti pot
Using a neti pot for the first time can feel awkward, but the process is simple once you know the steps. Herman outlines how to use one safely below.

Wash your hands first. Start with clean hands to avoid introducing germs to the device or your nose.Use the right water. Fill the neti pot with distilled, room temperature water, sterile water, or tap water that has been properly boiled and then cooled. Most neti pots on the market have a fill line to help prevent you from over-filling, if yours doesn’t, you should read the directions to determine how much water to add. Mix in the saline. Add the salt packet that comes with your neti pot to the water to create a safe-to-use saline solution. According to experts, if you don’t have ready made saline, you can mix together 1 cup of water with one quarter teaspoon of non-iodized salt (like kosher or canning salt).Get into position. Lean over the sink and tilt your head to the side.Rinse gently. Let the saline solution flow gently into one nostril and out the other. How the solution flows will depend on the device you are using. If your neti pot resembles a tea pot, you’ll need to tip it back to let the water pour out the spout. If you’re using a squeeze bottle, you can gently apply pressure. Or, if you are using an electric model, there should be a button for you to push.Clean up afterward. Wash the device and let it dry completely after each use.

If your neti pot resembles a tea pot, you’ll need to tip it back to let the water pour out the spout. If you’re using a squeeze bottle, you can gently apply pressure. Or, if you are using an electric model, there should be a button for you to push.
Clean up afterward. Wash the device and let it dry completely after each use.
Note: If your nose is completely blocked or the process is painful, don’t try to force the water through. Stop and consult with your doctor about other solutions to relieve congestion.
How to shop for a neti pot

Many neti pots look similar at first glance, but a few details make a big difference in how comfortable and easy one is to use. Design also comes down to personal preference. The features below can help you figure out what works best for you.

Material that’s easy to clean. Neti pots mostly come in ceramic and BPA-free plastic. Ceramic lasts longer and holds up to washing, while plastic is lighter and tends to be less expensive.  Whatever you choose, make sure you can clean every surface, since you’ll need to wash and dry the pot thoroughly after each use.A comfortable, well-shaped spout. The tip should be smooth and tapered so it fits snugly against your nostril without going in too far. A good seal keeps the saline flowing into your nose rather than dripping down your face, and a gentle, rounded tip is more comfortable for sensitive noses.The right capacity. Most adults do best with a pot that holds about 8 ounces, enough to rinse both nostrils in one fill, according to experts. Many kits come with premixed saline packets, which take the guesswork out of measuring. Just remember to mix them with distilled, sterile or previously boiled and cooled water, never water straight from the tap.

Whatever you choose, make sure you can clean every surface, since you’ll need to wash and dry the pot thoroughly after each use.

A comfortable, well-shaped spout. The tip should be smooth and tapered so it fits snugly against your nostril without going in too far. A good seal keeps the saline flowing into your nose rather than dripping down your face, and a gentle, rounded tip is more comfortable for sensitive noses.

The right capacity. Most adults do best with a pot that holds about 8 ounces, enough to rinse both nostrils in one fill, according to experts. Many kits come with premixed saline packets, which take the guesswork out of measuring. Just remember to mix them with distilled, sterile or previously boiled and cooled water, never water straight from the tap.
Is there anyone who should not use a neti pot?

Neti pots aren’t for everyone, and Salvador says a few groups should avoid them or check with a doctor first. People who’ve recently had ear or sinus surgery, or neurosurgical procedures performed through the ears or sinuses should skip them since the rinse can disrupt tissue healing and raise the risk of infection. He also says those with a history of ear infections may develop fluid behind the ears from using a neti pot.
Finally, Salvador says people with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of serious infection from improperly prepared water or a neti pot that hasn’t been cleaned well.
Frequently asked questions

Keeping your neti pot clean is just as important as using the right water, since a dirty device can introduce germs straight into your nose. “Follow the manufacturer’s cleaning instructions,” says Herman. “In general, wash the device thoroughly after each use and allow it to completely air dry before storing it.” Using regular dish soap is totally fine for most neti pots — and some are even dishwasher-safe (just check your specific model before putting it in there).

Drying it fully is the step that’s easiest to overlook. “You don’t want to leave moisture sitting inside the device because that can allow microorganisms to grow,” says Herman. Air drying is best, but if you are in a pinch, you can use a clean paper towel.

“They can,” says Herman. “Some people notice that their nose feels clearer immediately after an irrigation, particularly when there is a lot of thick mucus or congestion.” Just don’t expect a neti pot to make your cold disappear. “A neti pot isn’t curing the underlying cold,” says Herman. “Think of it as a way to rinse and moisturize the nose and remove mucus and irritants. It can provide symptomatic relief, but your body still needs time to recover from the viral infection.”

title: DHS watchdog refers its Corey Lewandowski investigation to Justice Department for review
summary: Lewandowski, the first manager on Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, was a top aide to then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem before she was fired.
story: The Department of Homeland Security inspector general has referred its investigation of former “special government employee” Corey Lewandowski to the Justice Department, according to a person familiar with the investigation.

The DHS investigation stems from questions about how a $220 million contract for an advertising campaign featuring then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem was awarded. At his Senate confirmation hearing, now-Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin testified in March that the department’s inspector general was looking into the contract.

That investigation then expanded, according to a source familiar with the matter, after NBC News reported that Lewandowski was alleged to have sought payment in exchange for protecting and growing the interests of a company, the GEO Group, that was seeking government contracts unrelated to the ad campaign.

In response to an inquiry from NBC News, Adam Trigg, an attorney for Lewandowski, said Thursday, “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity.”
The Wall Street Journal was first to report that the allegations are under review by the Justice Department.

Sources previously described to NBC News two meetings with the GEO Group at which Lewandowski asked the company to pay him, with one source saying he wanted a “success fee.” The GEO Group declined his requests.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

A spokesperson for Lewandowski in March denied that account of his interactions with the GEO Group. “This is absolutely false and did not happen — Mr. Lewandowski never demanded any payment or compensation from the Geo Group, at any time,” his representative said.

Before President Donald Trump fired her, Noem publicly admitted that she had personally approved the pricey contracts for the ad campaign but said Trump was aware of her involvement in their approval. After Noem was ousted, Trump told NBC News: “I wasn’t thrilled with it. I spent less money than that to become president. I didn’t know about it.”
Lewandowski was a top aide to Noem who departed from DHS after she left.

Reporting about allegations that Lewandowski requested payment from companies with business before DHS emerged only after Noem was fired and after Lewandowski, who was previously a top Trump adviser and the first manager of his 2016 campaign, left the department.
Weeks before she was fired, Noem also faced scrutiny for her attempts to procure a $70 million luxury jet for the department she led.

Asked about the referral of Lewandowski’s case to the Justice Department, Trump said Thursday: “I heard something about it, but I don’t know exactly what it is. All I know is I want my people to be honest, and if they’re not going to be honest, they have to be prosecuted.”
“I will never do anything to stop the prosecution of someone who’s dishonest,” he added.

title: The Sarah J. Maas Universe: How ‘ACOTAR,’ ‘Crescent City’ and ‘Throne of Glass’ Are Connected
summary: Before “A Court of Splintered Harmony,” revisit how Sarah J. Maas’ three series - “ACOTAR,” “Crescent City” and “Throne of Glass” - are connected in one universe.
story: 🚨 Spoilers ahead for Sarah J. Maas’ book series “Throne of Glass,” “A Court of Thorns and Roses” and “Crescent City.”
Before Sarah J. Maas releases the next novel in her “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series, many readers are revisiting the last story in which those characters appeared.
The only tricky element? That story was not a “Court of Thorns and Roses” book.

“A Court of Silver Flames” from 2021 is indeed the most recent book published in the “ACOTAR” series, but — and here comes the spoiler — some of those characters were last seen on the page in another series written by Maas: “Crescent City’s” third book from 2024, “House of Flame and Shadow.” That 850-page behemoth was the first to give a fuller scope at how all three of Maas’ fantasy series — “ACOTAR,” “Crescent City” and “Throne of Glass” — intertwine in one larger universe.
Here’s a deep dive into all the Easter eggs, callbacks and references that connect the three book series, ranging from the cryptic to the overt.
More on Sarah J. Maas

Sarah J. Maas Reveals Plans for Her Next Books — Including a 4th in the ‘Crescent City’ SeriesHow to Read All 18 of Sarah J. Maas’ Books in OrderSarah J. Maas Is BookTok’s Reigning Romantasy Queen. All RiseWho Is Koschei the Deathless? What to Remember About the Next ‘ACOTAR’ Villain
Sarah J. Maas Reveals Plans for Her Next Books — Including a 4th in the ‘Crescent City’ Series
How to Read All 18 of Sarah J. Maas’ Books in Order
Sarah J. Maas Is BookTok’s Reigning Romantasy Queen. All Rise
Who Is Koschei the Deathless? What to Remember About the Next ‘ACOTAR’ Villain
How ‘ACOTAR’ and ‘Throne of Glass’ Connect
The first explicit crossover between Maas’ series came in 2018, with the “Throne of Glass” finale, “Kingdom of Ash.”

As Aelin falls between worlds at the peak of her battle with the Valg, she passes through a “world of snowcapped mountains under shining stars” and sees two Fae: one winged male and one “heavily pregnant female.” The male notices her falling and sends his power, “like a gentle summer night,” to slow her down. This is Rhysand and Feyre, likely during the events of “A Court of Silver Flames,” which lines up with her pregnancy.

When “A Court of Silver Flames” published in 2021, some readers believed that moment was seen from the other perspective. In Chapter 62, after the annual Starfall event, a “rare red star” is spotted blasting across the sky and is interpreted as an “ill omen.”
How ‘ACOTAR’ and ‘Crescent City’ Connect
“Crescent City” more clearly establishes that the worlds of Maas’ three series are interconnected, starting with last line of the last chapter in Book 2, “House of Sky and Breath.”

At the end of “Crescent City” 2, heroine Bryce Quinlan confronts the Asteri, the rulers of her planet, Midgard. She learns they are not benevolent leaders but parasites who survive on firstlight generated by magical beings. When she learns the truth, she tries to use the Horn, which can open rifts between worlds, to go to Hel for help against the Asteri.

Instead she lands in another world, surrounded by Fae who believe her to be a threat. One of them looks eerily similar to her brother, Ruhn. When Bryce says her name, that Fae male responds: “Hello, Bryce Quinlan. My name is Rhysand.”
And there ends Book 2.

Book 3, “House of Flame and Shadow,” picks up where Book 2 leaves off. When Bryce lands in Prythian, Rhys and his Inner Circle interrogate Bryce. Soon they all learn that the Asteri, the primary villains in “Crescent City,” are the same as the Daglan, an evil force found in the history books of Prythian.

Readers learn in “A Court of Silver Flames” that the Daglan were vanquished by Rhys’ ancestors 15,000 years before the events of the books. But in “House of Flame and Shadow,” Bryce discovers that the Daglan escaped to Midgard to conquer a new planet and curate sources of power to serve as food. But they have maintained a desire to find a way back to their home world.

The ancient Fae relic known as the Horn is a big part of “Crescent City” lore. It’s first introduced in “House of Earth and Blood” when it goes missing from its place in Luna’s Temple. By the end of the book, readers learn Bryce’s best friend, Danika, had discovered the Horn’s ability to open doors between worlds, ground it into ashes, mixed it with ink and imbued it onto Bryce’s back as a tattoo when she was drunk. This was Danika’s effort to hide the Horn from the evil people looking for it and happened days before she was killed.

While Bryce is in Prythian in “House of Flame and Shadow,” she learns that the Horn is actually part of the Dread Trove, a collection of powerful artifacts made by the Cauldron. In a “Court of Silver Flames,” Nesta and the Night Court find the other three relics in the Trove — the Harp, the Crown and the Mask.

And speaking of missing artifacts — Bryce and the Night Court crew also learn in “House of Flame and Shadow” that Gwydion, a long-missing sword that’s a pair to spymaster Azriel’s dagger Truth-Teller, is none other than Bryce’s Starsword, a weapon in Midgard that can only be wielded by the chosen Starborn Fae.

In “House of Flame and Shadow,” Bryce at first tries to hide from the Night Court crew her tattoo that contains the Horn. The tattoo is written in a script Bryce doesn’t even know and is supposed to translate to, “Through love, all is possible.”

Amren is first to clock the tattoo and tells Rhys that Bryce’s tattoo is written in the same language found in “The Book of Breathings,” an object in the “ACOTAR” world with an ability to control the Cauldron. The book is also mysteriously mentioned in “House of Earth and Blood”; it’s in Jesiba Roga’s library alongside “The Walking Dead,” a book from “Throne of Glass.”

In “A Court of Mist and Fury,” Amren identifies the language in which “The Book of Breathings” is written as “Leshon Kadoesh” or “The Holy Tongue.” Rhys then shares that, according to legend, the language is one “of mighty beings who were here ... and then vanished.”

In “House of Flame and Shadow,” Bryce teams up with Nesta and Azriel to navigate a tunnel system near the Prison, led by the light from the glowing eight-pointed star on Bryce’s chest. One of the obstacles they face is the Middengard Wyrm, a large-toothed monster that Feyre faces in the first “ACOTAR” book.
But Bryce raises an interesting question when facing the creature.
“Middengard? Like — Midgard? Did they come from my world originally?” she asks, though Nesta and Azriel are unable to answer.

The theory of a lost Dusk Court was popular among “ACOTAR” fans, since it felt like a glaring omission from Prythian’s landscape. The continent has four seasonal courts — Spring, Autumn, Summer and Winter — and three solar courts — Night, Day and Dawn, but no Dusk.
It turns, it did once exist.

In “House of Flame and Shadow,” Bryce, Azriel and Nesta end up in the Prison via the tunnel system and find the same spot Nesta had found the Harp in “A Court of Silver Flames.” (The Harp was notably found on top of a “large rendering of an eight-pointed star.”) (Notably, Nesta has an eight-pointed star on her spine, and Bryce has one that glows on her chest.) (Also notably, a High Priestess in “Throne of Glass” has an eight-pointed star tattooed on her forehead.)

The three then encounter a hologram of Silene, the long lost daughter of Theia, a Fae queen and the original Starborn. Though Bryce already knew she is a descendent of Theia, Silene’s storytelling is how she learns that the Starborn Fae of Midgard had originated in Prythian.

According to Silene, Theia had served the Daglan for a long time while in Prythian, but eventually overthrew them and was able to claim her land — the island on which the Prison is located — for herself. That land thrived with “dusk, twilight — that’s what the island was in its long-buried heart.”

But after getting greedy for power, Theia and her court — as well as people with red hair who “looked alarmingly like Bryce’s father,” the Autumn King — migrated to Midgard, only to find themselves trapped under the reign of the very creatures they had fought to overthrow.

Silene was able to return to Prythian and escape the Asteri, but she concealed her power and the memory of ancestors vanished. The land of the former Dusk Court around her died, forming the barren isolation of the Prison. When Silene eventually married her mate, a High Lord of the Night Court, her firstborn son glowed with starlight inherited from her. “It was light of the evening star. The dusk star,” she says.
Bryce’s Starborn power is later described as a “dusk power,” a force the princes of Hel also call “starfire.”
How ‘Crescent City’ Connects to ‘Throne of Glass’

“House of Flame and Shadow” contains notable crossovers with “Throne of Glass,” Maas’ first series published in 2012. But many speculate that the world of “Crescent City” was first alluded to in “Kingdom of Ash,” the last book in the “Throne of Glass” series.

When Aelin falls between worlds — in the same instance she passes by Rhys and Feyre, as mentioned above — she also passes by a “world where a great city had been built along the curve of a river, the buildings impossibly tall and glimmering with lights.” It’s likely this is Lunathion, aka the titular Crescent City, which gets its name from the bend of the Istros River through it.
From there, though, most connections are seen in passing references and winks at the series.

The most overt connection between “Crescent City” and “Throne of Glass” comes in “House of Flame and Shadow” with the Under-King’s passing reference to Wyrd, which he describes as his home planet’s equivalent of Midgard’s Urd, the goddess of fate.

Wyrd, however, isn’t a goddess, but a “force that governed worlds. A cauldron of life, brimming with the language of creation,” says Under-King, the head of Lunathion’s Bone Quarter and leader of the House of Flame and Shadow.

In “Throne of Glass,” Wyrd, pronounced “word,” is indeed everywhere. The central conflict across the eight-book series centers on Aelin’s attempts to close the Wyrdgates, essentially portals between worlds (sound familiar?) by gathering all the Wyrdkeys. Her goal is to destroy the keys to prevent the Valg, demons that possess people and feed off their souls (again, sound familiar?), from coming to her world and conquering it with the power of Wyrdstone. She also learns to harness the power of Wyrdmarks, aka, magic runes.

It’s unclear if the Valg of “Throne of Glass” are the same as the Asteri/Dalgan, though both beings aim to conquer and consume. But “House of Flame and Shadow” does contain several references to the Asteri’s power over worlds as a “collar,” which is a major tool the Valg used to possess people, like Dorian.
After “House of Sky and Breath,” readers learned that shifters, including wolves like Ithan and Danika, are also Fae who just originated from a different world.

Once Ithan takes Hypaxia’s antidote to the Asteri’s power blocker in “House of Flame and Shadow,” he learns that his power wasn’t always just limited to shifting. He also has the power of wielding snow and ice.

The combination of an animal form and an elemental power is the prototype of the Fae found in “Throne of Glass,” suggesting shifters like Ithan came from the same world as Aelin. Fans of that series will remember Rowan Whitethorn could shift into a hawk and could wield wind.

Let’s also go back to the tale told by Silene, the daughter Queen Theia. When recounting to Bryce, Nesta and Azriel how Theia led a takeover of Midgard, she notes that the rifts opened once again and more Fae appeared “from another world this time.”

“They were Fae like us, but not,” Silene says. “The ears, the grace, the strength were identical, but they were shape-shifters, all of them. Each capable of turning into an animal. And each, even in their humanoid body, equipped with elongated canine teeth.”
Ithan, armed with his newly discovered powers, later takes on the Under-King directly.
